dilemma:
A river-basin authority must decide whether to prohibit commercial harvesting of living sphagnum from its headwater peat bogs for twenty years or renew existing licenses at their current commercially viable intensity. The licensed crews have complied with all rules, but continued removal repeatedly breaks the moss’s water-retaining surface before it can recover. Hummocks decline, peat dries more often, and the vegetation shifts toward a simpler sedge-dominated wet meadow. A ban would allow sphagnum carpets and hummock-and-hollow structure to recover, sustaining bog rosemary, cotton grass, sundews, native sedges, and specialist mosses as a characteristic native peat-bog plant community.

Twelve small contracting crews rely on this harvest for horticultural growing media. It provides roughly one-third of participating households’ annual income and supports several owner-operated firms whose specialized equipment has little value in other local work. Since these are the only moss deposits within economical hauling distance, a ban would end customer contracts, close several firms, and require workers to retrain, commute farther, or take less remunerative seasonal jobs. They would retain limited other earnings, social support, and transition assistance, but their established livelihoods would be substantially disrupted. Monitored trials found that reduced cutting, longer rotations, and small refuges could not maintain the bog’s water-retaining structure at any harvest level sufficient to keep the crews commercially viable.

Should the river-basin authority choose the harvest ban to protect the native plant community or renew the licenses to protect the crews’ livelihoods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Existing sphagnum carpets remain intact and cut areas gradually recover a continuous water-retaining surface and hummock-and-hollow structure. Those conditions allow bog rosemary, cotton grass, sundews, native sedges, and specialist mosses to persist or recolonize as a locally characteristic peat-bog plant community.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit all commercial removal of living sphagnum from the authority-managed headwater bogs for twenty years, the monitored minimum period needed for damaged moss carpets and hummock structure to recover substantially.
human_outcome_if_protected: The crews lose a substantial recurring income stream and cannot recover their equipment and business investments through local moss harvesting. Several owner-operated firms close, existing customer contracts end, and workers must retrain, commute farther, or accept less remunerative seasonal employment.
human_protective_option: Renew the existing crews’ licenses at the current commercially viable harvest intensity, preserving legal access to the only moss deposits within economical hauling distance.
novelty_signature: Authority-owned headwater peat bogs; horticultural sphagnum crews; direct harvest of the native community’s water-retaining foundation; monitored failure of commercial rotations; twenty-year recovery period; closure of specialized small firms without severe deprivation.
title: Headwater bog moss harvest

dilemma:
In a semi-arid interior basin, two remaining large tracts of native bunchgrass prairie are separated by a three-kilometre belt of irrigated forage-seed fields. The belt is the only area with the soil depth, slope, and elevation needed to restore the same prairie community between them. If a regional planning commission acquires the fields at market value, retires irrigation, removes leveling berms, restores natural microtopography, and seeds native grasses and forbs, a broad functional prairie belt will develop over roughly ten to fifteen years. It will provide cover, feeding sites, and breeding habitat for movement-limited grassland insects and small reptiles, allowing repeated movement, recolonization, and plant dispersal between the remnants. Keeping the fields in production leaves the remnants isolated by frequently cut crops, pesticide exposure, and bare service lanes.

The commission may instead retain the agricultural designation. That would preserve enough forage-seed acreage for the local cleaning plant to meet its minimum operating threshold, sustaining growers’ nearby processing, contractors’ work, employment, and retail demand in the service town. Although landowners would receive market-value payments if the fields were acquired, restoration would reduce seed volume below the plant’s threshold. The plant is expected to close, contractors would lose work, and seasonal and permanent earnings and commercial activity would decline persistently. Should the regional planning commission choose habitat restoration that reconnects the prairie remnants or retain irrigated seed production to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Over an expected establishment period of roughly ten to fifteen years, the restored belt becomes sufficiently wide and continuous to provide cover, feeding sites, and breeding habitat for movement-limited grassland insects and small reptiles. Native plants can also disperse incrementally through the belt. Repeated movement and recolonization reconnect populations in the two prairie remnants.
ecologically_protective_option: Acquire the central fields at market value, end irrigation and routine cultivation, remove field-leveling berms, restore natural microtopography, seed locally sourced native bunchgrasses and forbs, and control invasive plants until a broad belt of functional prairie links the two remnants.
human_outcome_if_protected: Landowners receive market-value acquisition payments, but removal of the central acreage reduces seed volume below the local cleaning plant's documented minimum operating threshold. The plant is expected to close, several contractors lose enough work to close or contract, and both seasonal and permanent earnings decline. The town experiences sustained underemployment and less predictable commercial activity, without loss of housing or essential services.
human_protective_option: Retain the belt's agricultural designation and irrigated forage-seed production, preserving enough cultivated acreage to support the town's seed-cleaning plant and associated contractor network, but forgo restoration of the connecting habitat.
novelty_signature: Semi-arid basin prairie bottleneck; irrigated forage-seed belt; irrigation retirement and microtopographic repair; broad resident-habitat corridor for insects, reptiles, and plants; documented seed-cleaning throughput threshold; compensated growers but persistent town-wide employment and business instability.
title: Restoring Prairie Through an Irrigated Seed District

dilemma:
In an Arctic archipelago, a storm has damaged the sheltered inlet harbor that supplies several remote settlements with fuel for household heating and diesel-generated electricity. The national government owns an adjacent raised beach containing the only aggregate tested as suitable and available in sufficient volume to rebuild the harbor for full-size seasonal fuel vessels. It can designate the parcel a no-quarry, no-industrial-use conservation zone or authorize quarrying and reconstruction.

Conservation would leave the inlet’s water exchange intact and prevent sediment from entering its shallows. Its kelp forests, capelin spawning grounds, soft-bottom benthic communities, seabird feeding areas, and seals would remain connected in their present functioning condition. If quarrying and the required breakwater proceed, fine sediment would settle on kelp holdfasts and capelin spawning substrate, while the narrowed inlet would retain more suspended material. Kelp and spawning habitat would contract, and the inlet would shift toward a less diverse, silt-tolerant benthic community with less prey support for fish, seabirds, and seals.

Without the full-size harbor, fuel must arrive by repeated small-barge shipments during a short calm-weather season. Heating and electricity prices would rise substantially, households and businesses would face fuel allocations, and nonessential commercial power would sometimes be cut. Minimum household heating and essential services would remain protected. Rebuilding the harbor would restore predictable fuel inventories, lower energy costs, and avoid routine limits. Should the national government choose the conservation zone that protects the marine ecosystem or authorize the quarry and harbor works that protect reliable energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The inlet remains in its present functioning condition: water exchange is not further restricted, quarry-derived sediment does not enter the shallows, and the connected kelp, spawning, benthic, seabird, fish, and seal relationships persist.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the raised beach as a no-quarry, no-industrial-use conservation zone, thereby preventing extraction of the aggregate required to reconstruct the harbor at its former full-size fuel-vessel capacity.
human_outcome_if_protected: Fuel must be delivered through repeated small-barge shipments during a short calm-weather season. Transport costs substantially raise heating and electricity prices, while limited annual throughput requires household and business fuel allocations and occasional scheduled cuts to nonessential commercial power. National reserves and priority rules preserve minimum household heating and uninterrupted power for clinics, emergency services, and other essential facilities.
human_protective_option: Authorize quarrying on the raised beach and use the aggregate to reconstruct the harbor with a breakwater and approach suitable for full-size seasonal fuel vessels.
novelty_signature: Arctic raised-beach aggregate restriction; storm-damaged seasonal fuel harbor; quarry sediment and breakwater-driven circulation change affecting a kelp-capelin-benthic food web; remote settlements relying on costly, capacity-limited small-barge energy deliveries.
title: Coastal gravel reserve or reliable fuel harbor

dilemma:
A public land-management authority controls the groundwater wells, spring-flow rights, bypass gates, and canal headworks serving a desert spring complex and nearby family-owned date groves. Four linked spring channels support an endemic hydrobiid snail found nowhere else. In critically dry years, reserving the first 1.8 million litres per day for the springs during the hottest eight weeks would keep every channel flowing, oxygenated, and below the snail’s lethal temperature boundary. The snail would continue to breed throughout its entire range and disperse among channels, preserving the biological distinctiveness of the spring complex.

That reservation would reduce irrigation deliveries to the groves. Roughly one-third of orchard acreage would experience persistently lower yields, and repeated dry-year reductions would shorten the productive lives of mature palms on that land. The owners would retain their homes, most production, and viable businesses, but would lose substantial crop income and capital value in long-established private orchards. If the authority instead provides full established dry-season deliveries, all mature palms can be maintained, preserving crop production, orchard longevity, and ordinary agricultural and market value. But the two lowest spring channels would become warm, stagnant pools, their snail populations would be lost, and the species’ occupied range would be reduced by about half.

Should the public land-management authority reserve water to protect the endemic snail across all four channels, or provide full deliveries to protect the date-grove owners’ established property use?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: All four spring channels remain flowing, oxygenated, and below the snail’s lethal temperature boundary. Breeding populations persist throughout the species’ complete geographic range, and water connections continue to permit dispersal and genetic exchange among channels.
ecologically_protective_option: During each critically dry year, reserve the first 1.8 million litres per day for continuous flow through the four spring channels during the hottest eight weeks, reducing deliveries to the date groves.
human_outcome_if_protected: The reduced irrigation causes persistently lower fruit yields on roughly one-third of the orchard acreage and, when the allocation recurs in dry years, progressively shortens the productive lives of mature palms on that acreage. Owners retain their homes, most production, and viable farm businesses, but lose substantial crop income and capital value embedded in long-established orchards.
human_protective_option: During those eight weeks, provide the groves with their full established dry-season delivery volume, leaving only the lower bypass flow that remains after agricultural deliveries.
novelty_signature: Desert spring-and-canal system; endemic hydrobiid snail occupying four linked channels; authority-held groundwater and spring-flow right; mature private date orchards with shortage-adjustable delivery contracts; continuous oxygenated-flow threshold versus recurrent loss of productive palms and orchard capital value.
title: Spring discharge reserved for an endemic snail

dilemma:
A century-old tidal dam encloses Heron Polder, where 64 lawful homes stand within the natural tidal frame. By excluding ordinary high tides, the barrier has turned a former estuary into a shallow freshwater impoundment dominated by limited freshwater plants and small fish. Marine nursery access, tidally renewed benthic prey, and regular feeding by larger estuarine fish and shorebirds are absent. If the dam is completely removed, twice-daily saline inundation and sediment exchange will restore salt-marsh vegetation, benthic invertebrates, juvenile-fish nursery use, and feeding access for larger fish and fish-eating birds, reestablishing a connected estuarine food web across the polder and adjacent bay.

Removal would also bring ordinary tides onto village roads, utilities, sewer infrastructure, and house floors, making permanent occupancy impossible. The environmental regulatory agency can require relocation before breaching, with acquisition, replacement housing, tenant protections, moving assistance, and reconstructed community facilities in a nearby purpose-built neighborhood on higher ground. Yet residents would permanently lose their current homes, historic village site, familiar landscape, and exact place-based relationships. Renewing and rehabilitating the dam would allow them to remain safely in their homes and preserve their daily-support networks, but the estuarine food web would not return. Gate schedules, a ring levee, and elevating homes cannot both protect present residence and substantially restore the food web. Should the environmental regulatory agency remove the dam to protect trophic integrity or renew it to protect residents’ continued residence?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Restored tidal exchange reestablishes salt-marsh producers, benthic invertebrate prey, juvenile-fish nursery use, and feeding access for larger predatory fish and fish-eating birds across the polder and adjacent bay.
ecologically_protective_option: Revoke the barrier permit, require complete removal of the tidal dam, restore unrestricted tidal exchange, and relocate all residents to a nearby purpose-built neighborhood on higher ground with full housing and moving support.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents receive secure replacement homes nearby and may move together with reconstructed community facilities, but they permanently lose their current dwellings, historic village site, familiar landscape, and exact place-based networks.
human_protective_option: Renew the barrier permit and require rehabilitation of the dam, thereby excluding ordinary tides and allowing residents to remain safely in their current homes and village.
novelty_signature: Inhabited coastal polder behind a tidal dam; ordinary-tide inundation rather than exceptional storm risk; restoration of a salt-marsh plant–benthic invertebrate–juvenile fish–predatory fish and bird food web; nearby collective relocation; protective gate schedules truncate essential feeding tides, while a ring levee consumes the only high-marsh band.
title: Breaching the tidal dam at Heron Polder

dilemma:
A municipal council must decide the future of a low floodplain where community allotments occupy the narrow strip between two remnant oxbow wetlands. Drainage ditches and low berms allow cultivation but keep this only restorable connection dry, interrupting movement of water, sediment, organic matter, seeds, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates. Monitoring shows that the smaller wetland’s shallow-water vegetation and amphibian occupancy are declining as its populations remain isolated. If the council designates the floodplain as a protected area, ends the licenses after notice, removes berms, and plugs the ditches, seasonal flows will reconnect the oxbows. The basins will again function as a continuous wetland complex with a broader range of characteristic habitats and communities.

The allotments, however, provide low-income residents in nearby apartment blocks with a substantial share of their fresh vegetables, and surplus is exchanged with neighbors. If cultivation ends, compensation will cover tools and approved improvements but not recurring harvests. Gardeners will have to buy higher-priced produce from nearby shops or take a long bus trip to a discount market, reducing the variety and regularity of fresh vegetables and making familiar crops harder to obtain. Staple foods will remain available. Renewing the licenses would preserve this nearby, inexpensive food source, but ditch clearing and cultivation would maintain the ecological break.

Should the municipal council designate the protected area to restore wetland continuity or renew the allotment licenses to protect residents’ food access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Seasonal inundation again crosses the former allotment strip. Wetland vegetation recolonizes the connector, and water, sediment, organic matter, seeds, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates can move between the oxbows. The two basins resume functioning as a connected wetland complex, supporting recolonization after ordinary local disturbances and a broader range of characteristic wetland habitats and communities.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the entire municipal floodplain as a protected area, end the allotment licenses after the required notice period, compensate license holders for tools and approved improvements, remove the low berms, and plug the drainage ditches so seasonal flows can reconnect the two oxbows.
human_outcome_if_protected: Gardeners lose the only nearby ground suitable for food cultivation. Compensation covers tools and plot improvements but does not replace recurring harvests. Households must purchase more expensive produce locally or make long bus trips to the discount market, reducing the variety and regularity of fresh vegetables and making culturally familiar crops harder to obtain. Staple foods remain available, and the burden does not create starvation, homelessness, or serious health danger.
human_protective_option: Decline protected-area designation and renew the allotment licenses, allowing continued cultivation, berm maintenance, and ditch clearing so residents retain nearby access to inexpensive fresh vegetables.
novelty_signature: Municipal oxbow floodplain; low-income community allotments occupying the only shallow hydrological connector; shared drainage and plot berms maintain a dry ecological break; protected-area designation requires rewetting and cultivation closure; affordable fresh-vegetable access conflicts with restoration of organism, seed, sediment, and organic-matter exchange.
title: Floodplain allotments or a continuous oxbow marsh

dilemma:
A landslide has destroyed the only vehicle road to an ancestral cemetery and ceremonial clearing used by families from dispersed mountain villages. A narrow path remains, but it requires about six hours of steep walking each way. Many elders and residents with limited mobility can no longer attend the annual three-day vigil, and walkers cannot carry the food, tools, and ceremonial materials needed for grave cleaning, shared meals, sung histories, and teaching younger participants at the graves. Without vehicle access, the vigil survives only in a smaller, age-selective form.

An intermunicipal public authority has approved a replacement road across the intact slope surrounding the cemetery. Construction would remove mature trees, old soils, roots, and deadwood from a centuries-old cloud forest. The permanent opening would increase sunlight and wind, reduce humidity, eliminate epiphyte-bearing host trees, and divide continuous interior habitat for decades. The route study found that every safe vehicle alignment crosses this same broad forested slope. Ending the road at the forest margin would still leave four to five hours of steep walking and would not restore access or material transport. The only lower route lies in the active landslide runout, while tunnel portals, spoil, and equipment areas would also occupy old-growth forest. Moving the gathering to a village would permit commemoration but eliminate the grave cleaning and graveside recitation that partly constitute the practice.

Should the authority cancel the replacement road to protect the old-growth cloud forest, or construct it to protect the community's traditional graveside practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The forest retains its closed canopy, persistently humid interior, mature epiphyte-bearing trees, deadwood and decomposer processes, and uninterrupted cover used by forest-dependent animals. The limited existing footpath remains but is not widened or converted into a vehicle corridor.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the planned replacement road and retain only the existing narrow pedestrian path, avoiding a new vehicle corridor through the old-growth cloud forest.
human_outcome_if_protected: Physically able residents can still reach the cemetery on foot, but many elders and people with limited mobility cannot participate there. The carrying limits and travel time also sharply reduce shared meals, grave-tending work, and attendance by whole families. The vigil survives only in a smaller, age-selective form, weakening the intergenerational transmission of place-specific songs and histories.
human_protective_option: Construct the replacement road, restoring practical vehicle access close to the cemetery so residents of varied ages and abilities can conduct the full communal vigil at its traditional graveside location.
novelty_signature: Centuries-old mountain cloud forest enclosing an ancestral cemetery; landslide destroyed vehicle access but left a six-hour footpath; intermunicipal authority considers cancelling a replacement road; road edges would dry humid forest and remove mature epiphyte hosts; cancellation makes a three-day graveside vigil age-selective and undermines grave tending, sung histories, shared meals, and intergenerational participation.
title: Cloud-forest access road and the annual graveside vigil

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to permit annual basin-wide systemic herbicide treatment in a state-owned reservoir’s only sheltered sailing and paddling basin. Dense hydrilla mats have spread through the launch lanes, instruction circuit, and assisted capsize-recovery area, making them unusable. Treatment at the concentration and duration supported by agency trials would suppress hydrilla enough to keep the basin navigable for sailing instruction, adaptive paddling, recovery practice, and regular small-craft recreation. The reservoir’s other arms have stronger wind, wakes, and motor traffic and cannot provide equivalent conditions; without treatment, hydrilla will again cover the usable basin within two growing seasons, ending these programs and regular use of the sheltered water.

Yet hydrilla is interwoven with native pondweed that includes distinct warm-shoal and deep-water ecotypes. Several heat- and depth-associated alleles are concentrated in the warm-shoal plants. Repeated systemic-herbicide exposure would eliminate most flowering warm-shoal plants and sharply reduce their recruitment. Although deep-water pondweed would remain, the reservoir would lose the ecotype holding most of its warm-shoal and heat-associated alleles. Prohibiting treatment would preserve viable breeding stands across the depth gradient, along with their differentiated alleles and continuing gene exchange. Agency trials and site constraints have ruled out lower-dose, mechanical, spatial, and relocation alternatives that would avoid these consequences.

Should the agency prohibit systemic herbicide treatment to protect the pondweed’s genetic diversity, or authorize it to protect established sailing and adaptive-paddling recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The warm-shoal and deep-water pondweed ecotypes retain viable breeding stands across the depth gradient. Their differentiated alleles and continuing gene exchange preserve the reservoir population’s range of heat- and depth-associated traits.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit systemic aquatic-herbicide treatment within the sheltered basin, preventing repeated non-target exposure of the native pondweed ecotypes.
human_outcome_if_protected: Within two growing seasons, hydrilla again forms continuous mats over the usable basin. Launching, routine maneuvering, and organized recovery practice become impracticable, causing sailing instruction and adaptive paddling programs to leave the reservoir and ending regular small-craft use of that sheltered water.
human_protective_option: Authorize annual basin-wide systemic-herbicide treatment at the concentration and duration shown by agency trials to suppress hydrilla enough to keep the launch lanes, instruction circuit, and assisted-recovery area usable.
novelty_signature: State reservoir’s uniquely sheltered small-craft basin; genetically verified warm-shoal and deep-water pondweed ecotypes interwoven with hydrilla; systemic aquatic-herbicide permit supported by multi-year treatment trials; loss of heat-associated genetic variation versus sailing instruction and adaptive-paddling access.
title: Aquatic herbicide in a sheltered sailing reservoir basin

dilemma:
A regional government must decide whether to cancel a planned causeway-and-bridge link between a populated island and the mainland. Most of the crossing would be solid embankment, leaving only a short bridge over the navigation channel. If built, the embankments would close most of the shallow sound's tidal cross-section. Flow would scour eelgrass near the bridge, while reduced circulation would deposit sediment behind the causeways and narrow tidal channels. The continuous shallow-water route linking the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries would be broken, disrupting juvenile fish movement and invertebrate dispersal.

Cancelling the project would preserve tidal exchange and connected habitat. Islanders would retain safe, subsidized, year-round passenger and vehicle ferries, but would continue to face fares, queues, busy-period bookings, sailing intervals, limited vehicle space, an overnight gap, and occasional weather reductions. Building the link would allow direct road, bus, bicycle, and pedestrian travel at any hour. Several culverts would still concentrate flow and leave depositional zones. A fully elevated bridge needs long grades for navigation clearance, but the island approach reaches the existing village before the bridge could return to ground level; a lower bridge would obstruct navigation. Closely spaced foundations in deep soft sediment would also disturb eelgrass and redirect shallow flow. Ferry subsidies cannot provide spontaneous overnight vehicle travel.

Should the regional government cancel the fixed link to protect habitat connectivity, or build it to protect islanders' mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Twice-daily tidal exchange remains distributed across the full width of the shallow sound. Water, suspended sediment, fish, larvae, and dispersing invertebrates continue moving among the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries, preserving the sound as a connected habitat system.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the fixed link and maintain the subsidized year-round passenger-and-vehicle ferry under its existing service pattern.
human_outcome_if_protected: Islanders retain safe, year-round mainland access, including vehicle transport, but remain subject to fares, advance planning, loading queues, finite vehicle space, sailing intervals, an overnight service gap, and occasional weather-related timetable reductions. These constraints continue to burden irregular shifts, evening education, family visits, shopping, and spontaneous trips.
human_protective_option: Build the causeway-and-bridge link, allowing direct road, bus, bicycle, and pedestrian travel without ferry fares, loading queues, sailing intervals, vehicle-capacity limits, or overnight timetable gaps.
novelty_signature: Cool-water tidal sound connecting an outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries; cancellation of a causeway-and-short-bridge fixed link; hydraulic constriction fragments aquatic habitat through localized scour and sheltered deposition; populated-island residents retain a subsidized vehicle ferry but continue to face fares, booking limits, waits, and overnight mobility constraints.
title: Cancel the Inish Sound Fixed Link

dilemma:
A remote Indigenous coastal community operates salmon pens in a shallow lagoon under its marine tenure. Eelgrass around the pens supports an amphipod found nowhere else. When recurring sea-lice outbreaks exceed mandatory fish-health thresholds, the elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to permit a crustacean-targeting bath pesticide. Tarpaulins contain treatment during dosing, but the spent water must then be released. In the weakly flushed lagoon, it reaches every occupied eelgrass bed and kills amphipods faster than they reproduce. Repeated treatments would drive the species to extinction.

If the council denies permits, affected pens must be harvested early, emptied, and fallowed. Lower harvest weights and idle periods reduce production, interrupt processing, and cause rotating layoffs, fewer shifts, and lost vessel and maintenance contracts. Income guarantees and housing and utility protections prevent severe deprivation, but do not restore dependable work or commerce. Timing treatment outside breeding periods does not solve the problem because multiple amphipod life stages remain year-round and lice outbreaks are not seasonal. Treating fewer pens still contaminates every bed, onboard filtration has not reached a safe concentration, the nearest licensed receiving facility is beyond the vessels' range, and the council's tenure and certified moorings do not permit moving the pens offshore.

Should the council deny pesticide permits to protect the endemic species, or authorize discharge to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The endemic amphipod avoids pesticide exposure at lethal and reproduction-impairing concentrations and continues reproducing throughout the lagoon’s eelgrass beds, preserving a species found nowhere else.
ecologically_protective_option: Deny permits for use and discharge of the crustacean-targeting bath pesticide in the lagoon. When lice exceed the mandatory fish-health threshold, require affected pens to be harvested early, emptied, and fallowed rather than chemically treated.
human_outcome_if_protected: Recurring early harvests and mandatory fallowing reduce harvest weight, interrupt processing schedules, and leave pens idle. The resulting production decline causes rotating layoffs, fewer processing shifts, loss of vessel and maintenance contracts, and unstable revenues for community businesses. Community income guarantees and utility protections prevent homelessness, hunger, or loss of essential services, but do not restore dependable work or commercial activity.
human_protective_option: Authorize in-pen tarpaulin bath treatments and the subsequent permitted release of spent treatment water into the lagoon, allowing stocked fish to remain in production through their planned harvest cycle.
novelty_signature: Remote northern Indigenous marine tenure; community-owned salmon pens in a weakly flushed lagoon; lagoon-endemic eelgrass amphipod exposed to discharged crustacean-targeting bath pesticide; tarpaulin containment only during dosing; lice thresholds force early harvest and fallowing; linked instability across processing, vessel services, maintenance, and local commerce.
title: Aquaculture pesticide decision in an enclosed northern lagoon

dilemma:
Several upland villages maintain a centuries-old spring sheep drive from valley farms to common summer grazing grounds. Families walk the inherited multi-day route together, observing rituals at stopping places, sharing meals, and teaching route-specific herding knowledge to younger participants. The route has twelve unavoidable stream and ford crossings within a headwater protection district. Steep slopes, unstable banks, and the absence of alternative passage rights prevent rerouting, and temporary bridges cannot span most of the crossings. Because tick pressure is high, veterinary movement rules allow the prolonged, close-contact drive only when flocks receive an effective full-duration treatment. The only locally registered treatment that works for the full journey is a persistent synthetic-pyrethroid dip applied at licensed facilities in the district.

If a regional planning commission issues seasonal permits for the dip, residues from treated fleece will enter the low-flow streams through rain and repeated crossings; keeping treated sheep entirely out of the water is infeasible. Sensitive aquatic arthropods will suffer major losses, reducing leaf-litter processing and aquatic prey production. Trout recruitment will weaken, while dippers and insectivorous bats will lose productive feeding areas, diminishing the connected headwater food web.

If the commission denies the permits, flocks may be transported by truck to enclosed summer grazing, retaining flock ownership and grazing access. But the walked drive, its stopping-place rituals, and its intergenerational teaching will cease. Should the regional planning commission deny the permits to protect headwater trophic integrity, or issue them to protect the villages’ cultural practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Mayflies, caddisflies, freshwater crustaceans, and other stream invertebrates remain abundant enough to process leaf litter and graze algae while supplying prey to juvenile trout, dippers, and insectivorous bats. These producer, detritivore, prey, and predator relationships remain functional across the headwater network.
ecologically_protective_option: Deny seasonal permits for the persistent synthetic-pyrethroid sheep dip at facilities within the headwater district, preventing its use before the traditional drive.
human_outcome_if_protected: Regional veterinary movement rules do not allow flocks with the prevailing tick burden to undertake the prolonged, close-contact drive without an effective full-duration treatment. The animals may instead be transported directly by truck to inspected enclosed summer grazing, so families retain their flocks and grazing access, but the walked drive and its route-specific rituals and teaching cease.
human_protective_option: Issue a seasonal permit allowing the licensed pre-drive treatment, enabling adequately treated flocks to complete the traditional multi-day route.
novelty_signature: Upland communal transhumance; inherited route rituals; regulated pre-drive sheep dip; pyrethroid release from fleece at unavoidable headwater crossings; detritivore–trout–dipper–bat food-web disruption.
title: Sheep-dip restriction on a transhumance route

dilemma:
Cedar Ravine contains a temperate rainforest of centuries-old trees, layered canopy, nurse logs, specialist lichens, and moisture-dependent forest-floor communities. Although its canopy survives, the municipal downhill-cycling park has compacted trail corridors, drainage cuts, bridges, berms, and cleared sightlines that divide the understory and alter water movement. If the municipal council permanently closes the park and restores the area, it can remove the trail structures, regrade drainage cuts, loosen compacted soil carefully, replace woody debris, and replant native understory. These measures would reconnect forest-floor habitat, disperse runoff, reduce erosion and drying around old-tree roots, and restore the moist, shaded conditions on which the ravine’s old-growth assemblage depends. They would protect an irreplaceable long-established ecosystem, though they cannot recreate its ancient trees.

Closing the park would also remove the only nearby advanced downhill network used several times each week by local riders and a youth club for technical riding, exercise, instruction, competitions, and social gatherings. Gentler municipal paths remain available, and some riders could travel more than an hour to comparable facilities, but those alternatives cannot sustain the club’s regular advanced training and events. Retaining the complete system would preserve this affordable local recreational community, but continued riding and maintenance would keep the corridors compacted and drainage concentrated, progressively weakening the ravine’s humid, connected forest-floor processes.

A municipal survey found that any continuous advanced descent would cross saturated old-tree root zones, so retaining even one route would preserve a principal compacted corridor and leave restored areas hydrologically divided. Should the municipal council choose restoration that protects the old-growth ecosystem or continued operation that protects local downhill recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Restoration reconnects damaged forest-floor habitat, disperses runoff, reduces erosion and drying around old-tree roots, and reestablishes moist understory and deadwood conditions. It does not recreate the ancient trees; rather, it protects the surviving old-growth structure and restores supporting processes damaged by the trail network.
ecologically_protective_option: Permanently close the downhill park; remove bridges, berms, hardened turns, and artificial drainage features; regrade drainage cuts; loosen compacted soil without damaging surviving major roots; replace locally sourced woody debris; and replant native understory species. Allow only a short perimeter walking path outside the restoration area.
human_outcome_if_protected: Riders lose their only nearby advanced downhill network, and the youth club loses the site that supports its regular training, events, and social life. Members can still cycle on gentler municipal paths, and some can travel to distant downhill facilities, but those alternatives do not sustain the same skilled activity or convenient club program.
human_protective_option: Retain and maintain the complete interconnected downhill system, including the graded descents, bridges, hardened turns, sightlines, and drainage structures needed for safe advanced riding and organized events.
novelty_signature: Municipal temperate-rainforest ravine with surviving centuries-old canopy; youth and community downhill cycling; restoration of compacted technical trail corridors; conflict driven by altered drainage, old-tree root-zone erosion, and fragmentation of humid forest-floor habitat.
title: Restore the forest floor beneath Cedar Ravine’s downhill park

dilemma:
A river-basin authority must decide whether to cancel a planned secondary embankment along a broad Central European river. The embankment would keep ordinary overbank floods from reaching twenty-nine privately owned hay parcels, equipment sheds, and two seasonal farm shops. Without it, shallow, forecastable floods will continue to disrupt harvests, require equipment to be moved and buildings cleaned, temporarily block customer access, and reduce rental and resale values. The properties are not primary residences and remain usable, but their established agricultural and commercial uses will remain materially unreliable.

Cancelling the project would leave the active floodplain connected to moderate floods. Those floods deposit and expose fresh, moist sediment where seeds from numerous European black poplar trees can establish. This process sustains the basin’s last large naturally reproducing stand, preserving rare genotypes and creating new genetic combinations as older trees die. If the embankment is built, the recruitment area will no longer receive the sediment-bearing floods that create these seedbeds. Sexual recruitment will largely cease, and replacement will depend mainly on vegetative shoots from a limited number of surviving genotypes, progressively reducing this population’s documented genetic breadth.

Should the river-basin authority cancel the embankment to protect the black poplar population’s genetic diversity, or construct it to protect the owners’ reliable use and value of their property?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Moderate floods continue exposing and depositing fresh moist sediment across changing parts of the floodplain. Seeds from many parent trees can establish in different years and locations, allowing the population to retain rare genotypes and generate new genetic combinations as its older trees die.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the proposed embankment, leaving the floodplain compartment open to the moderate overbank floods, sediment deposition, erosion, and channel-edge movement needed for continued sexual recruitment of black poplar.
human_outcome_if_protected: The owners retain title and can continue farming and operating the seasonal businesses, but they continue to face recurring harvest disruption, equipment-moving and cleanup costs, temporary access loss, and depressed rental and resale values.
human_protective_option: Construct and maintain the embankment, excluding ordinary floods from the private parcels and making their established hay production, equipment storage, and seasonal retail uses substantially more reliable.
novelty_signature: Central European active-floodplain embankment cancellation; sexually recruited black-poplar genetic breadth; sediment-bearing overbank flows and transient seedbeds; hay parcels, equipment sheds, and seasonal farm shops; recurrent shallow-flood impairment of lawful property use.
title: Cancel the Lower-Floodplain Embankment

dilemma:
A public land-management authority must set the winter allocation from a limited reservoir above a desert canyon. If it releases enough water continuously to keep two broad gravel sills wetted, all of the canyon’s perennial pools will remain connected by flowing water and moist channel margins. Native minnows will be able to disperse and recolonize pools after local losses, aquatic-insect larvae will drift between reaches, and riparian amphibians will move through the canyon. This continuing exchange sustains demographic and genetic connections among populations that otherwise become isolated.

That choice would release much of the water outside the hours when electricity is most needed. Two isolated plateau towns would then have to buy more expensive regional power up to the capacity of their sole transmission link. Households would face sustained winter bill increases, while workshops and cold-storage businesses would operate under scheduled evening load limits and lose productive time. Essential heating, refrigeration, medical equipment, emergency services, and basic household electricity would remain guaranteed.

Alternatively, the authority can retain the disputed water and release it mainly during morning and evening peaks. The towns would receive their full expected winter electricity supply, avoiding import surcharges and recurring business constraints. But the gravel-sill reaches would dry for prolonged intervals, separating the pools for most of the winter and reducing recolonization, movement, and genetic exchange across the canyon. Should the public land-management authority choose continuous baseflow to protect habitat connectivity, or peak-timed hydropower to protect the towns’ affordable, reliable energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: All canyon pools remain connected by flowing, wetted reaches throughout winter. Native minnows can disperse and recolonize pools after localized losses, aquatic-insect larvae can drift between reaches, and riparian amphibians can move through continuously moist channel habitat. These movements sustain demographic exchange and gene flow among populations that would otherwise remain isolated.
ecologically_protective_option: Allocate enough stored water to maintain the surveyed minimum continuous baseflow through the canyon for the entire winter, keeping the gravel sills wetted and connecting all perennial pools. The release remains continuous even during low-demand hours rather than being concentrated into peak-generating periods.
human_outcome_if_protected: Some continuous releases generate electricity, but much of it occurs when local demand is low and the constrained intertie cannot export the surplus or import an equivalent amount at the evening peak. The releases also leave less stored water and lower hydraulic head for later dispatch. The towns therefore buy more expensive regional electricity up to the intertie limit. Households incur a sustained, material winter bill increase, while workshops and cold-storage businesses follow scheduled evening load limits and lose some productive operating time. Guaranteed minimum supply preserves essential heating, refrigeration, medical equipment, emergency services, and basic household electricity.
human_protective_option: Retain the disputed water in the reservoir and release it through the turbines mainly during morning and evening demand peaks. This preserves reservoir head and dispatchable generation but allows the reaches across the gravel sills to dry for prolonged intervals between releases.
novelty_signature: Desert canyon refuge pools connected across gravel-sill flow thresholds; winter allocation between continuous ecological baseflow and peak-timed storage hydropower; native minnows, aquatic insects, and riparian amphibians; isolated plateau towns with a constrained grid intertie; off-peak generation mismatch, reduced reservoir head, and protected essential electricity.
title: Winter baseflow through a desert canyon

dilemma:
On a small inhabited limestone island, the national government must decide the future of the only undeveloped parcel adjoining the cargo wharf. The parcel contains the island’s largest contiguous native coastal limestone scrub community, where salt-tolerant shrubs, endemic herbs, ground orchids, and seasonal annuals grow across shallow calcareous soils from the exposed shore to sheltered inland pockets. Designating it a permanent no-build reserve would preserve its characteristic species composition, seed banks, runoff patterns, and coastal-to-inland zonation.

The alternative is to authorize a refrigerated food depot with cold-storage rooms, a loading apron, fire access, drainage, utilities, and secure road access. Construction would remove most of the scrub through soil stripping and bedrock grading; altered drainage, vehicle disturbance, and weeds would leave disconnected margins dominated by disturbance-tolerant plants. Yet the depot would allow imported vegetables, fruit, dairy products, and other perishables to move directly into powered cooling. Reduced heat exposure and handling would lower prices and make these foods more consistently available to low-income residents, who currently face recurrent multiday stock gaps, higher costs, less varied shelf-stable diets, and extra shopping trips.

Should the national government designate the parcel as a permanent ecological reserve or authorize the depot to improve reliable, affordable access to perishable food?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The island's largest remaining contiguous limestone scrub community retains its characteristic species composition, shallow calcareous soils, seed banks, runoff patterns, and coastal-to-inland zonation.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the entire scrub parcel as a permanent ecological reserve and prohibit buildings, grading, paving, utility trenches, vehicle access, and construction drainage within it.
human_outcome_if_protected: Basic calories and shelf-stable staples remain available, and perishables continue to reach the island. However, spoilage and handling costs keep ordinary fresh foods markedly more expensive, while vegetables, fruit, and dairy products continue to experience recurrent multiday stock gaps. Households with limited incomes or transport rely more heavily on less varied shelf-stable diets and make additional shopping trips when shipments are divided among stores.
human_protective_option: Authorize construction and operation of a refrigerated depot on the parcel, including the minimum cold-storage rooms, loading apron, fire-access lane, drainage system, utility connection, and secure road access required for food handling and port safety.
novelty_signature: Small inhabited limestone island; contiguous wharf-side native coastal scrub; break-bulk perishables requiring shipment-scale immediate refrigeration; food-price and stock-gap effects from warm repeated transfers; shallow-soil removal, altered runoff, fragmentation, and weed-edge conversion.
title: Limestone scrub reserve or island food depot

dilemma:
A remote Indigenous community’s elected governing council must decide how to manage beavers in a boreal peatland surrounding an inherited cluster of twelve permanent homes on a low gravel ridge. Three beaver dam complexes have raised water across shallow peat divides, joining formerly intermittent ponds into a perennial wetland corridor. As long as the colonies and dams persist, the corridor retains connected sedge and willow habitat, movement routes for amphibians and aquatic invertebrates, waterfowl use, nutrient exchange, and pathways for recolonization among ponds. Yet the same impoundments keep groundwater above the surveyed limits for the homes’ foundations and wastewater fields.

The council can prohibit all community harvesting of beavers in the three-dam complex and relocate the households to completed higher-ground homes near the main village, with moving assistance and compensation. No one would be left homeless or in unsafe housing, but the move would permanently end residence in the established ridge cluster beside relatives, the meeting house, and family places. Alternatively, the council can authorize a recurring managed harvest and dam breaching sufficient to keep the homes within habitation standards. The households could remain safely in their current community, but the dams would no longer maintain the impoundments: peat between the ponds would dry seasonally, and the wetland corridor would become separate basins with reduced exchange of water, organisms, and ecological processes.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the harvest ban that protects wetland continuity or the managed harvest that protects the households’ continued residence?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Resident beaver colonies and their dams persist. Water remains impounded across the shallow divides, preserving perennial hydrological links, saturated sedge and willow habitat, organism movement, nutrient exchange, and recolonization pathways across the multi-pond wetland system.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit hunting, trapping, or other taking of beavers throughout the three-dam pond complex, enforce the closure against community harvesters, and move the twelve households to completed higher-ground homes with moving expenses and compensation.
human_outcome_if_protected: No household becomes homeless or remains in an unsafe structure: residents move before the documented groundwater threshold is reached and receive completed replacement homes, compensation, and moving assistance. They nevertheless lose their current homes, immediate ridge neighborhood, daily proximity to the meeting house, and place-based routines.
human_protective_option: Authorize a recurring, council-managed beaver harvest at the three residentially relevant dam complexes, followed by dam breaching as needed, at a level sufficient to prevent resident colonies from rebuilding the impoundments and to keep groundwater below the ridge's habitation thresholds.
novelty_signature: Boreal Indigenous peatland settlement; beaver-harvest ban; three dam complexes maintaining hydrological and biological continuity across shallow peat divides; raised groundwater disabling lawful ridge homes and wastewater fields; compensated collective move to nearby higher ground.
title: Beaver-harvest decision in a boreal peatland settlement

dilemma:
A regional government must decide the future of an obsolete irrigation dam above a Mediterranean delta. Although a newer off-channel system supplies downstream irrigation, the old reservoir traps nearly all coarse sand and gravel from the catchment. Removing the dam through staged drawdown would release suitable stored sediment gradually and allow future bedload to reach the coast. Waves and currents would again distribute material across the delta front, lagoon entrances, and shallow seabeds, reducing the sediment deficit, supporting shallow sand habitat and lagoon margins, and slowing erosion and fragmentation along exposed seagrass edges. The restored process would strengthen the connected marine habitat mosaic used by seagrass-edge communities, infauna, nursery fish, lagoon organisms, and their predators.

Retaining the dam would keep the reservoir at its stable managed level. That would preserve the lake-based economy of a nearby delta town: campsites, rowing clubs, cafés, equipment rentals, and seasonal events, along with the maintenance contractors, suppliers, retailers, and employees they support. Removal would replace the lake with a narrower, seasonally variable river corridor; the existing rowing courses, campsites, launching areas, and event venues could no longer operate in their current locations. Visitor spending would decline, some small firms would close or become seasonal, and workers and owners would face job changes and less predictable incomes.

Should the regional government remove the dam to protect the marine ecosystem or retain it to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Staged removal releases suitable stored sand and gravel without a single uncontrolled sediment pulse, and future bedload again reaches the coast. This reduces the delta's sediment deficit, supports renewal of shallow sand habitat and lagoon margins, and slows erosion and fragmentation along exposed seagrass edges. It does not prevent all retreat caused by storms or sea-level rise, but it restores a major material process linking the river, delta, lagoons, and nearshore ecosystem.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the obsolete dam through a staged drawdown and monitored decommissioning program, manage the initial release of stored sediment, and thereafter allow natural coarse-sediment transport from the catchment to the delta and nearshore marine system.
human_outcome_if_protected: Removal permanently replaces the level reservoir with a narrower, seasonally variable river corridor. The existing rowing courses, shoreline campsites, launching areas, and lake-event venues can no longer operate in their current locations. Visitor spending declines, several small firms close or become seasonal, supplier turnover falls, and affected workers and owners face job changes and less predictable incomes.
human_protective_option: Retain the dam and its managed, stable reservoir level, preserving the established lake-based recreation, hospitality, and service economy.
novelty_signature: Mediterranean sediment-starved delta; removal of an obsolete irrigation dam; staged release and renewed transport of coarse bedload to lagoon entrances, seagrass edges, and shallow marine nursery habitat; town-wide reservoir recreation economy dependent on a stable lake surface.
title: Freeing Sediment for the Cala Verde Delta

dilemma:
Four municipalities share the Orenda estuary, whose narrow central reach contains the entire known range of the Orenda burrowing goby. This endemic fish breeds by excavating burrows in exposed, soft vertical banks. High-speed passenger ferries use the narrows on the fastest public-transport route from residential towns to the main employment and rail center. Their wakes undercut and slump the banks faster than natural deposition can rebuild them, destroying nests during breeding and leaving too little intact habitat for the following season. Continued high-speed operation reduces occupied habitat below the level associated with stable recruitment.

The intermunicipal public authority can designate the narrows as an aquatic protected area and require ferries to travel at displacement speed year-round. That rule would keep wakes below the bank-failure threshold, allowing breeding burrows, eggs, and juvenile shelter to persist across the goby’s only occupied reach. Ferry travel would continue, but approximately 3,100 regular passengers would face crossings about 22 minutes longer, less practical rail transfers, and less frequent evening service. They use the route for work, education, appointments, and family travel; an indirect road route remains available. Alternatively, the authority can leave the corridor outside the protected area, retaining fast crossings, existing evening frequency, and coordinated rail connections while the goby’s breeding habitat continues to decline.

Should the intermunicipal public authority designate the protected area and impose the speed rule, or continue high-speed ferry service to protect passengers’ mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Lower-energy wakes allow the soft bank faces to remain intact between natural renewal events, preserving breeding burrows, attached eggs, and shallow juvenile shelter throughout the endemic goby’s only occupied reach. Monitoring indicates that this amount of stable bank habitat supports continued recruitment.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the goby’s breeding narrows as an aquatic protected area and require every passenger ferry to remain at displacement speed throughout the protected reach year-round, keeping wakes below the measured threshold for failure of the nesting banks.
human_outcome_if_protected: Ferry service continues, but each crossing takes about 22 minutes longer. Some coordinated rail transfers cease to be practical, evening service becomes less frequent, and regular users incur substantial recurring losses of time and schedule flexibility. An indirect road route remains available.
human_protective_option: Leave the ferry navigation corridor outside the protected area and continue licensing the existing high-speed service and coordinated rail timetable.
novelty_signature: Four-municipality estuary narrows; endemic soft-bank burrowing goby; aquatic protected-area speed condition; ferry-wake threshold causing year-round nesting-bank failure; slower commuter crossings, fewer rotations, and disrupted rail transfers.
title: No-Wake Reserve in the Orenda Narrows

dilemma:
A county seeks permits for a permanent haul road across a spring-fed limestone basin connecting public roads to privately managed woodland. The basin contains an intact native calcareous-fen community of sedges, orchids, low shrubs, and marl-pool plants. Its continuous vegetation mosaic depends on low-nutrient groundwater spreading diffusely through shallow peat and marl. A raised, compacted road embankment would interrupt that flow, while cross-drains would concentrate it at isolated points. Part of the fen would become drier and another part more persistently flooded and nutrient-enriched; reeds and woody vegetation would expand as specialized fen plants decline, converting much of the basin into reedbed, scrub, and simplified wetland patches.

Several logging crews and family woodland operators depend on the woodland beyond the basin for a substantial recurring share of their income. They need dependable access for harvesting equipment, timber trucks, and rescue vehicles to maintain selective-harvest rotations and regular crew employment. Without the road, steep and rocky approaches cannot safely accommodate those vehicles, and the stands would no longer be commercially harvestable. Contracts, crew hours, and family woodland income would decline durably, though the affected people would retain their homes and some work or income elsewhere.

The environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to deny the indispensable permits, cancelling the road and preserving the native fen community, or approve them and protect the operators’ established livelihoods: should it choose the ecologically protective option or the option protecting the human interest?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Groundwater continues to spread through the basin at its existing levels and rates. The connected assemblage of wet hollows, marl-pool margins, sedge and orchid areas, and slightly drier shrub islands remains intact rather than being divided into hydrologically different sections.
ecologically_protective_option: Deny the indispensable permits, thereby cancelling the permanent haul road and preserving the fen's diffuse groundwater movement, low-nutrient conditions, and continuous native vegetation mosaic.
human_outcome_if_protected: Without a haul road, the woodland stands beyond the fen cannot be reached by the harvesting, loading, and rescue vehicles required for safe commercial operations. Those stands cease to be economically harvestable, causing a durable reduction in harvest contracts, crew hours, and family woodland income. The affected people retain their homes and some work or income from other stands, so the burden does not amount to destitution or total occupational displacement.
human_protective_option: Approve the permits and allow construction of the haul road, giving operators regular equipment and truck access needed to continue established selective-harvest rotations and associated employment.
novelty_signature: Spring-fed limestone fen; cancellation of a permanent forestry haul road; embankment and cross-drains disrupting diffuse calcareous groundwater flow; conversion of sedge-orchid-marl vegetation to reedbed and scrub; selective-timber crews and family woodland operators losing recurring income because steep alternate approaches cannot support harvesting or rescue vehicles.
title: Cancel the limestone-fen timber access road

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
During an unusually severe dry season, a state or provincial natural-resources agency must allocate the remaining freshwater held by a barrage at the head of a subtropical estuary. Releasing the entire pool down the estuary would keep the salt front below an old-growth freshwater tidal swamp of centuries-old bald cypress and swamp tupelo. Freshwater conditions would preserve its elevated organic root islands, shaded channels, and long-established amphibian, epiphyte, soil-biota, and decomposition processes. If the agency instead diverts the pool to irrigation canals, saline water will occupy the swamp during the critical interval. Much of the salt-intolerant understory would die, mature trees would suffer extensive fine-root mortality, and later erosion would convert much of the old-growth freshwater swamp into younger brackish marsh; restoring freshwater next year would not quickly restore its mature trees, soils, or continuity-dependent assemblages.

The same pool is the minimum seasonal allocation needed for a licensed rice-and-pulse district to complete its crops. Diverting it would maintain mill throughput and regular, inexpensive deliveries to discount grocers in a nearby industrial city, where many low-income households rely on these familiar staples. Releasing it for the swamp would cancel irrigation deliveries and cost the district one harvest. Imports and assistance would preserve adequate calories, but for roughly a year staple prices would rise, neighborhood stores would have recurring stock gaps, and households with limited budgets and shopping options would need to spend more, travel farther when possible, or substitute other foods.

Should the agency choose the ecological release that protects the old-growth swamp or the irrigation allocation that protects reliable access to affordable staple food?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The release maintains freshwater soil conditions around mature cypress and tupelo roots, preserves the elevated root islands and shaded channels, and sustains the amphibian, epiphyte, soil-biota, and decomposition processes associated with centuries of ecological continuity.
ecologically_protective_option: Release the remaining dry-season pool down the estuary at the sustained rate required to keep the salt front below the old-growth freshwater swamp, cancelling the district's irrigation deliveries for that growing season.
human_outcome_if_protected: The irrigation district loses one harvest. Regional imports prevent hunger and keep basic calories available, but limited milling, warehousing, and discount-distribution capacity means imports do not fully replace the local volume on its normal schedule. For roughly one year, rice and pulse prices rise appreciably, discount grocers experience recurring stock gaps, and low-income households must spend more, travel farther when possible, or substitute away from familiar low-cost staples. Existing food assistance offsets some expense but does not eliminate availability gaps or all added costs.
human_protective_option: Divert the remaining pool into the irrigation canals, enabling the district's rice and pulse crops to mature and maintaining the established low-cost urban supply, while allowing saline water to occupy the swamp during the critical dry-season interval.
novelty_signature: Old-growth freshwater tidal cypress–tupelo swamp; finite barrage pool allocated between estuarine salt-front repulsion and rice-and-pulse irrigation; salinity-driven fine-root mortality followed by root-island erosion; low-income industrial-city households dependent on discount-grocery staples; one-year affordability and stock-reliability burden.
title: Dry-season freshwater for an old-growth tidal swamp forest

dilemma:
A public land-management authority must decide how to manage an obsolete logging corridor through recovering caribou winter range. The corridor is designated and groomed as a public snowmobile trail linking a small service settlement to lawful cabin leases. Grooming and repeated passage create a firm lane through deep snow, allowing wolves to travel efficiently into areas where soft snow otherwise gives caribou some spatial separation. Its open, browse-rich edges also support deer, which can sustain wolves near caribou habitat. Closing the route, roughening its surface, restoring drainage, and re-establishing native conifers and shrubs would end the maintained snow lane and gradually restore denser boreal habitat. This would reduce artificial predator access and deer subsidy, improving the functioning relationships among winter forage, caribou, deer, and wolves, though it would not guarantee caribou recovery.

The authority can instead retain the direct route, preserving a roughly 25-minute one-way winter trip for cabin leaseholders, maintenance workers, and settlement residents making maintenance, social, and same-day visits. If the corridor is restored, every lease remains accessible by a plowed public road, but each one-way trip would take about 80 minutes, adding roughly 110 minutes to a round trip, increasing fuel use, and making evening or short visits harder. Should the public land-management authority restore the corridor to protect trophic integrity or keep it groomed to protect winter mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Closure and surface roughening immediately prevent recreation from maintaining a continuous packed-snow lane. As conifers and shrubs recover over subsequent years, the corridor becomes less efficient for wolf travel and less favorable to deer-associated edge browse. These changes reduce two sources of altered predation pressure in caribou winter habitat and help restore the spatial relationships among lichens and other winter forage, caribou, deer, and wolves. The measure improves food-web function but does not guarantee caribou population recovery.
ecologically_protective_option: End grooming and motorized use of the corridor, decompact and roughen the former roadbed, restore blocked drainage, and establish native conifers and shrubs so that the strip progressively returns to dense boreal habitat rather than remaining a linear travel lane and browse-rich edge.
human_outcome_if_protected: Every cabin remains legally and physically accessible, but routine winter travelers must use the road around the forest. A round trip takes about 110 minutes longer, consumes more fuel, and becomes harder to fit into evenings or short same-day windows. The recurring burden reduces convenient access for maintenance, social visits, and ordinary use of the leases without depriving anyone of housing, essential services, or sole access.
human_protective_option: Keep the corridor designated, groomed, and maintained as the direct winter snowmobile route between the settlement and cabin area.
novelty_signature: Boreal obsolete logging corridor used for lawful winter cabin access; snow-surface decompaction and conifer-shrub restoration; elimination of a wolf travel lane and deer prey subsidy; lichen–caribou–deer–wolf trophic relationships; safe but roughly 110-minute-longer round-trip road access.
title: Restoring a packed winter-access corridor in caribou range

dilemma:
A national government must decide the future of an obsolete storm-control dam in a coastal reserve. Replacement defenses now protect the coast, but the dam still holds a former tidal creek as a stable freshwater lagoon. Removing the dam and excavating its compacted foundation would restore the creek’s full tidal opening, reconnecting upper marsh channels, saltmarsh pools, the estuary, and the sea. Daily tidal exchange would allow juvenile mullet, gobies, prawns, migratory eels, and other mobile aquatic organisms to move among feeding, refuge, nursery, and overwintering habitats.

Keeping the dam would preserve a popular accessible fishing site. Older anglers, disabled anglers using purpose-built level platforms, and family groups rely on its calm water, stable levels, nearby parking, and sheltered space for small non-motorized boats. Other local fishing waters do not provide the same combination of access and predictable conditions. But retaining the dam would continue excluding ordinary tides and restricting movement between the impounded creek, upper marsh channels, and estuary.

Removal would end the stocked freshwater fishery: changing depths, currents, exposed mud, and salinity would make the existing platforms unusable in their present form and prevent the lagoon from remaining a stable freshwater venue. Should the national government remove the dam to restore habitat connectivity or retain it to protect accessible angling?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Daily tidal exchange reconnects saltmarsh pools and upper channels with the estuary. Juvenile mullet, gobies, prawns, migratory eels, and other mobile aquatic organisms can move with changing tides among feeding, refuge, nursery, and overwintering habitats.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the dam and excavate its compacted foundation, restoring the creek’s full tidal opening and unobstructed exchange between the upper marsh channels, estuary, and sea.
human_outcome_if_protected: The stable freshwater lagoon disappears. Twice-daily depth changes, currents, exposed mud, and salinity shifts make the existing platforms unusable in their present form and end the stocked freshwater fishery. Although some users could fish elsewhere or use redesigned tidal platforms, many regular participants would lose the calm, predictable form of angling they can use independently or with minimal assistance.
human_protective_option: Retain and maintain the dam at its existing freshwater operating level, preserving the calm lagoon and its accessible angling facilities.
novelty_signature: Obsolete storm-control dam in a national coastal reserve; restoration of tidal-prism connectivity among remnant upper marsh channels, estuary, and sea; juvenile fish, prawns, and migratory eels; loss of a stable freshwater lagoon used for accessible angling by older and disabled recreationists.
title: Open the Tidal Creek or Preserve the Accessible Angling Lagoon

dilemma:
An Indigenous community’s ancestral coastal cemetery occupies the last intact stabilized dune in its territory. Its remaining unoccupied burial plots overlap the only wild population of a genetically distinct lineage of a regionally widespread dune violet. Flowering plants and a persistent seed bank extend across nearly all stable ground suitable for additional graves. Each excavation, along with spoil placement and new access paths, would destroy rooted plants and buried seeds. As plots are used, the remaining patches would become too sparse and separated for reliable pollen exchange and recruitment, ultimately eliminating this distinct local lineage and its rare alleles.

Families have an established tradition of burying relatives beside ancestors in the coastal cemetery. An accessible inland community cemetery can accommodate future burials and allows funerals and local interment to continue, but it cannot provide continuity with the existing ancestral graves. Closing the coastal plots would permanently end this place-based form of ancestral burial for future relatives. Continuing approvals until the plots are occupied would allow the practice to continue for those families receiving them, while destroying most of the violet lineage’s sole habitat.

The elected Indigenous governing council administers both cemeteries and can either close the remaining coastal plots, protect the dune, and direct future burials inland, or continue approving coastal burials. Should the council choose the ecologically protective closure or the option that protects families’ ancestral burial practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The only wild population of the violet lineage remains intact, retaining its rare local alleles, persistent seed bank, flowering density, and pollen exchange across the small dune habitat.
ecologically_protective_option: Close all remaining coastal-dune plots to new graves, protect the intact dune surface from further excavation and new access paths, and direct future burials to the inland community cemetery.
human_outcome_if_protected: Families can still conduct funerals and bury relatives locally at the accessible inland cemetery, but future relatives cannot be interred beside ancestors in the coastal cemetery. The community consequently loses the continuing, place-based form of its ancestral burial practice.
human_protective_option: Continue issuing burial approvals in the ancestral coastal cemetery until the remaining usable plots are occupied, allowing families receiving those plots to continue interment beside their ancestors.
novelty_signature: Indigenous ancestral coastal cemetery on the last intact stabilized dune; continued interment beside ancestors; cemetery-plot restrictions; grave excavation and access paths destroy a violet seed bank and disrupt pollen exchange; loss of a sole genetically distinct plant lineage while inland burial remains available.
title: New burials in an ancestral dune cemetery

dilemma:
On a humid volcanic island, the only high-voltage line from a geothermal plant to six eastern villages crosses roadless cloud-forest gullies. Three headwater streams beneath the corridor contain the entire known population of an endemic stream salamander. Under the current pesticide license, persistent broadleaf herbicide is applied to maintain conductor clearances. Wet-season storms carry residues and contaminated sediment into the streams at concentrations that kill salamander larvae and their aquatic invertebrate prey. Recruitment fails in the two most affected streams, leaving a single small, isolated population vulnerable to drought, disease, and storms.

The regional government can instead prohibit the herbicide and require rope-access manual cutting during planned de-energization periods. This would allow breeding to continue in all three streams and preserve connectivity across the salamander’s complete known range. Yet manual cutting would triple vegetation-management costs and require about eighteen planned four-hour daytime shutdowns each wet season. Higher regulated tariffs and repeated interruptions would disrupt refrigeration, home working, retail activity, and small electric machinery for households, shops, and workshops, though protected essential loads would remain supplied. Continuing the existing applications would retain current tariffs and continuous daytime power while preserving required conductor clearances.

Should the regional government choose the herbicide prohibition that protects the endemic salamander or continued applications that protect reliable, affordable energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Herbicide residues in storm runoff fall below concentrations known to kill salamander larvae and aquatic invertebrate prey. Successful breeding can continue in all three streams, maintaining connectivity across the species' complete known range.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit use of the persistent broadleaf herbicide throughout the transmission corridor and require the operator to control vegetation by rope-access manual cutting during planned de-energization periods.
human_outcome_if_protected: Slow rope-access cutting triples the corridor's vegetation-management cost and requires approximately eighteen planned four-hour daytime shutdowns over each wet season. The resulting tariff increase and interruptions disrupt refrigeration, home working, retail activity, and use of small electric machinery, although protected essential loads remain supplied.
human_protective_option: Continue tightly scheduled corridor applications under the existing license, allowing the operator to maintain conductor clearances at the current frequency and cost without recurring vegetation-related shutdowns.
novelty_signature: Humid volcanic island cloud forest; endemic stream salamander confined to three transmission-corridor headwaters; regulation of persistent right-of-way herbicide; storm-driven larval and prey toxicity; roadless rope-access cutting requiring wet-season de-energization; village tariff increases and planned daytime outages.
title: Herbicide control beneath an island transmission line

dilemma:
Across a river basin’s glacial plain, a twelve-kilometre chain of seasonal prairie potholes is connected by shallow grassed swales running through seven family-owned grain farms.
