A river-basin authority can designate the potholes, swales, and necessary hydrological buffers as a protected wetland complex. If it does, spring sheet flows and varied wetland conditions will persist across the chain, sustaining shallow-water, mudflat, grass, and sedge habitats. Aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, and breeding waterbirds will continue to use the wetlands as a connected system, including for movement and recolonization after drought years.

Designation would also permanently prohibit drainage and cultivation within the mapped areas. The families would retain their homes, ownership, and viable farm operations, but protected strips and wet pockets would reduce workable acreage and machinery efficiency. Their recurring income, resale value, borrowing value, and freedom to decide future uses of portions of their land would decline.

If the authority declines designation, the owners may install tile systems permitted under ordinary agricultural rules and cultivate the swales. They could drain persistently waterlogged ground, consolidate fields, improve machinery use, stabilize yields, and preserve the ordinary productive and financial value of their property. Yet tile drainage would eliminate several intermediate potholes, shorten inundation in others, and leave surviving basins hydrologically isolated, with simplified seasonal habitats and fewer opportunities for amphibians and aquatic invertebrates to move across the chain. Should the river-basin authority designate the protected wetland complex or decline designation to protect the families’ property interests?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The linked seasonal wetland system retains its spring sheet flows and varied hydroperiods. Alternating shallow-water, mudflat, grass, and sedge habitats persist, and aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, and breeding waterbirds continue to use the chain as a connected complex rather than isolated ponds.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the entire pothole-and-swale chain as a protected area, prohibit new tile drainage within the mapped complex and buffers, and require the connecting swales to remain under permanent vegetation.
human_outcome_if_protected: The families retain ownership, residences, and viable farm operations, but permanently lose drainage and cultivation options on the designated portions. Irregular protected strips and wet pockets reduce workable acreage and machinery efficiency, causing recurring income losses and lowering resale and borrowing value.
human_protective_option: Decline protected-area designation and allow the owners to install tile systems that comply with existing agricultural permits and cultivate the swales, preserving contiguous field use and the ordinary productive and financial value of their property.
novelty_signature: Glacial prairie-pothole chain across privately owned grain farms; protected-area designation covering seasonal basins, shallow swales, and hydrological buffers; tile drainage intercepting perched groundwater and disrupting post-drought recolonization; recurring losses of workable acreage, machinery efficiency, collateral value, and owner control.
title: Prairie pothole chain across family cropland

dilemma:
Five coastal towns share an Atlantic inlet where mature blue-mussel reefs provide the principal persistent hard substrate amid mobile sand and mud. The reefs are built from living mussels, bound shell, and accumulated shell layers. Their recovery would restore substantial vertical and spatial complexity, supporting attached algae, worms, small crustaceans, juvenile fish, and feeding birds, while strengthening filtration, biodeposition, nutrient exchange, and resistance to winter disturbance. Monitoring shows that six consecutive years without removal of large mussels would allow surviving beds to form the bound shell layers needed for this recovery.

Twenty-four licensed hand gatherers from long-established fishing families depend on wild mussels for a substantial share of household income. The lowest annual catch that covers operating and purification costs and maintains regular restaurant and wholesale orders would keep their occupation viable, preserving their skills, licenses, arrangements, and buyers. Yet that catch would continue removing large mussels and new structure faster than multilayered reefs can form, leaving shallow, patchy beds vulnerable to winter burial and dislodgment. A six-year inlet-wide ban would end all legal wild catch; closure payments and seasonal work would meet basic needs but would not preserve full income, active commercial gathering, or established customer relationships.

Should the intermunicipal public authority impose the six-year harvest ban to protect the marine ecosystem, or continue the commercially viable harvest to protect the gatherers’ livelihood?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Mussel beds regain substantial vertical and spatial complexity, creating more persistent hard substrate across the soft-bottom inlet. This supports attached algae, worms, small crustaceans, juvenile fish, and feeding birds while increasing filtration, biodeposition, nutrient exchange, and resistance of the reef community to winter disturbance.
ecologically_protective_option: Impose a six-year inlet-wide ban on taking wild blue mussels. Monitoring indicates that six consecutive years without removal of large mussels would allow surviving beds to accumulate multiple bound shell layers, retain recruits, and become substantially more resistant to winter disturbance and burial.
human_outcome_if_protected: Gatherers receive no legal wild-mussel catch for six years. They lose substantial earnings, routine use of specialized skills, and established customer relationships; restaurants and wholesalers shift to farmed or outside suppliers. Time-limited closure payments and secondary seasonal work prevent hunger, homelessness, and unmanageable debt but do not keep commercial mussel gathering active.
human_protective_option: Continue authorizing the lowest inlet-wide annual catch that can cover gatherers' operating and purification costs and maintain recurring restaurant and wholesale orders, thereby keeping commercial hand gathering viable.
novelty_signature: Five-town Atlantic inlet; licensed wild blue-mussel hand gatherers; large-mussel removal prevents accumulation of byssally bound shell layers on mobile sand and mud; winter burial and dislodgment maintain a simplified marine community; six-year inlet-wide harvest ban conflicts with the minimum catch needed to preserve purification arrangements and local buyer relationships.
title: Mussel-Reef Harvest Closure in a Shared Atlantic Inlet

dilemma:
In an inland arid basin, groundwater-fed alkali meadows beside a small town contain a characteristic mosaic of saltgrass, sedges, rushes, and native forbs. Their wet-to-dry zonation depends on groundwater remaining above several spring outlets. Current permitted pumping for local irrigation keeps groundwater near or below those elevations. If an environmental regulatory agency renews present allocations without reserving water for the springs, most meadow surfaces will lose spring-fed moisture. Sedges and moisture-dependent forbs will progressively disappear as salt accumulation expands bare patches and shrubs and disturbance-tolerant weeds replace much of the meadow mosaic.

The same aquifer supports dairies and feed-growing operations, along with repair shops, suppliers, and haulers. These lawful businesses depend on predictable irrigation production, and their workers and owners have organized employment, contracts, loans, and income around longstanding permits. The agency can instead impose a basin-wide pumping limit for at least ten years, reserving enough groundwater to sustain spring discharge and the meadow community. That decision would reduce irrigation allocations, contract fodder production and herd capacity, and is expected to lead one dairy and several feed-growing operations to close or cease local production. Recurring work and business income would decline for several years, although transition payments and support would prevent acute deprivation. Renewing current allocations would preserve established production, shifts, contracts, and local trade, while allowing the meadow springs to fail.

Should the environmental regulatory agency choose the ecological groundwater reserve that protects the native plant community or renew current allocations to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Continuous or seasonally reliable spring discharge is maintained or restored as groundwater heads recover. The meadows retain their wet-to-dry zonation, allowing saltgrass, sedges, rushes, and moisture-dependent native forbs to persist, reproduce, and resist conversion to shrubs, weeds, and saline bare ground.
ecologically_protective_option: For at least ten years, set the basin pumping limit low enough to reserve the groundwater needed to keep the water table above the meadow spring outlets, proportionally reducing existing irrigation allocations while monitoring groundwater head and spring discharge.
human_outcome_if_protected: Reduced irrigation supply contracts fodder production and herd capacity. One dairy and several feed-growing operations are expected to close or cease local production, recurring work for suppliers and haulers declines, and the town experiences several years of lower and less predictable employment and business income. Transition payments prevent acute deprivation but do not preserve the former volume of recurring local trade.
human_protective_option: Renew current irrigation allocations without an ecological groundwater reserve, preserving existing agricultural production while allowing groundwater levels to remain below the elevations needed to supply several meadow springs.
novelty_signature: Arid inland aquifer allocation; native alkali-meadow moisture and salinity zonation; groundwater-head threshold at multiple spring outlets; dairy, feed-growing, haulage, and repair economy; ecological groundwater reserve versus renewal of irrigation allocations.
title: Desert-basin spring meadows or the agricultural service economy

dilemma:
On a cool oceanic peninsula, two rows of 28 legally built, permanently occupied cottages stand on the only sand-covered saddle linking intact foredunes to inland dune slacks. The saddle once carried windblown sand between these areas. Its foundations, retaining walls, roads, buried utilities, gardens, and sand fencing now interrupt that movement. As a result, older slacks accumulate organic matter and scrub without being replaced by young slacks, leaving the peninsula-endemic sand earwig with a small peripheral population and a progressively reduced range of breeding and drought-refuge habitat.

A regional planning commission can either approve a funded managed-retreat and restoration plan or renew permanent residential status and utility protection for the block. Restoration would require acquiring all cottages at replacement value, providing moving expenses and comparable homes in nearby towns, and removing the structures and obstructions so the saddle can be regraded. Seasonal sand transport would then resume, producing shifting dry dunes, disturbed sand, and moist young slacks used by the earwig. Residents would retain access to employment and services but would lose their current homes, coastal setting, and compact mutual-aid community.

Renewing residential protection would allow every household to remain, preserving familiar surroundings and neighbor-support arrangements. Yet the stabilized saddle would remain, and the principal habitat-forming process for the endemic species would stay disabled. Should the regional planning commission choose habitat restoration for the sand earwig or protect the residents’ ability to remain in their homes?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Seasonal sand transport resumes across the saddle, periodically burying vegetation and creating new low hollows that intersect the water table. This restores a shifting mosaic of sparsely vegetated dry dune, recently disturbed sand, and moist young slacks used by the endemic sand earwig for breeding, foraging, and drought refuge.
ecologically_protective_option: Adopt the funded managed-retreat and restoration plan; acquire all 28 cottages at replacement value; provide moving expenses and comparable replacement homes in nearby towns; remove buildings, foundations, retaining walls, roads, buried utilities, gardens, and sand fencing; and regrade the saddle so windblown sand can again move between the foredunes and inland slacks.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents receive replacement-value payments, moving support, and comparable replacement housing in nearby towns, preserving access to employment and essential services and preventing homelessness. They nevertheless must leave their current cottages, lose their immediate coastal setting, and cannot preserve the compact block as an intact residential and mutual-aid community.
human_protective_option: Renew permanent residential status and public utility protection for the cottage block, preserving every household’s ability to remain in its current home while retaining the fixed, stabilized dune saddle and foregoing process-based restoration there.
novelty_signature: Cool-oceanic peninsula cottage block occupying the sole dune saddle; peninsula-endemic sand earwig; process-based restoration of wind-driven foredune-to-slack sediment movement; foundations, retaining walls, utilities, and stabilization interrupt shifting slack formation; compensated relocation dissolves a compact coastal mutual-aid neighborhood.
title: Recreating a mobile dune field beneath an occupied seafront block

dilemma:
A remote river city's municipal council must decide the future of the lowest lock-and-dam on its freight canal. The structure creates the navigation pool that lets shallow-draft barges deliver flour, rice, pulses, and cooking oil directly to the central food terminal. Removing it would force smaller truck shipments from a distant railhead over a long mountain route, raising prices and causing recurring stock gaps. Residents would still have enough food, but staples would be less affordable and accessible, especially for low-income households and people unable to reach distant supermarkets.

The dam divides a native sturgeon population into two small breeding groups that retain different uncommon alleles. The operating lock provides no reliable upstream passage and little downstream juvenile passage. Removal would restore recurring movement and interbreeding; retention would allow genetic drift to narrow the population's inherited traits. Scheduled lock openings do not work: telemetry shows that adults do not reliably enter the lock, while juveniles disperse when its gates remain closed. The only low-gradient bypass corridor is occupied by the terminal apron and floodwall, whose removal would itself end barge unloading. A new railhead terminal is also unavailable because its direct approach crosses a weight-restricted historic bridge, while the adequate route requires the same long mountain detour.

Should the council remove the lock-and-dam to protect sturgeon genetic diversity, or retain it to protect reliable, affordable access to staple foods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Recurring migration and interbreeding reconnect the breeding groups, allowing alleles retained on either side to circulate through the combined river population and reducing further loss of genetic variation through drift and unequal reproductive success.
ecologically_protective_option: Decommission and remove the lock-and-dam, restoring a continuous river reach through which adult sturgeon can move between spawning areas and juveniles can disperse in both directions.
human_outcome_if_protected: Bulk staples must instead be moved from a distant railhead in smaller truck shipments. Added transfer and transport costs produce sustained price increases, while smaller and less frequent loads cause recurring multi-day stock gaps at neighborhood shops. Residents retain access to sufficient food, but ordinary staples become less affordable and practically available, especially for households unable to travel to distant supermarkets.
human_protective_option: Retain and maintain the lock-and-dam so the navigation pool continues supporting direct bulk-food deliveries to the municipal terminal.
novelty_signature: Remote municipally chartered freight canal; lock-and-dam dividing two small breeding groups of long-lived native sturgeon; bidirectional migration limiting drift-driven allele loss; navigation pool enabling direct bulk-staple barges; distant rail-to-truck substitution causing sustained food-price increases and neighborhood stock gaps.
title: Sturgeon gene flow versus a municipal grain-barge pool

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
A state or provincial natural-resources agency must decide whether to cancel a planned tidal-energy barrage across the narrow mouth of a northern macrotidal bay. The barrage would restrict the volume and timing of tidal exchange, reducing tidal range and current velocities. Feeding flats would no longer drain normally, fine sediment would accumulate over suspension-feeding beds, bottom-water flushing would weaken, and movement between the bay and open sea would be obstructed. Benthic prey, migratory fish, and diving birds would decline across a marine ecosystem whose flats, channels, marshes, and food web depend on natural tidal processes.

Cancelling the project would preserve the bay’s tidal range, reversing currents, salinity exchange, sediment transport, oxygen renewal, and seasonal movement of marine organisms. Yet six coastal towns would remain dependent on an aging transmission line, imported power, and costly oil-fired generators during winter peaks. Essential electricity and heating would continue through protected circuits and backup supply, but households and businesses would face higher bills, recurring conservation periods, scheduled curtailments of nonessential loads, and reduced operating hours for some energy-intensive businesses.

If the agency proceeds, predictable tidal generation would cover the towns’ modeled winter shortfall, reduce oil use, lessen curtailments, and support more affordable electricity, heating, and commercial activity. Hydrodynamic modeling indicates that openings large enough to preserve the tidal prism and peak currents needed for normal drainage, sediment transport, and flushing would leave too little hydraulic head and turbine throughput to cover that shortfall. Should the agency cancel the barrage to protect the marine ecosystem or build it to protect energy access for the coastal towns?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Natural tidal exchange continues to maintain the extent and drainage of feeding flats, channel geometry, sediment sorting, bottom-water oxygenation, and seasonal migration routes. These processes sustain the bay as an integrated marine food web.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the planned barrage, preserving the bay’s natural tidal range, reversing currents, salinity exchange, sediment transport, oxygen renewal, and movement of marine organisms.
human_outcome_if_protected: Essential electricity and heating remain available through protected circuits, imported power, and oil-fired backup. However, households and businesses continue to face materially higher energy bills, recurring winter conservation periods, scheduled curtailment of nonessential loads, and reduced operating hours for some energy-intensive local businesses.
human_protective_option: Build and operate the barrage. Its predictable tidal-cycle generation, coordinated with imported power and existing backup units, would cover the towns’ modeled winter energy shortfall over the operating cycle, reduce oil generation, and relieve capacity-based curtailments.
novelty_signature: Northern macrotidal bay; cancellation of a provincially owned tidal-energy barrage; tidal-prism and hydraulic-head thresholds linking generation to bay-wide flats, channels, benthos, migratory fish, and diving birds; six coastal towns retaining costly oil backup and scheduled nonessential winter curtailments.
title: Cancel a tidal-energy barrage across a macrotidal bay

dilemma:
A municipal council must decide whether to ban the uprooting, cutting, and collection of native marram throughout a migrating dune neck that contains the only direct road between an outer residential district and the town center. If it adopts the ban and retires the road, windblown sand will bury the unused carriageway and marram will spread across it. This will create continuous vegetated dune substrate between northern and southern habitats, allowing flightless sand-running beetles, dune spiders, and other ground-dwelling dune specialists to disperse without crossing an exposed road corridor.

If the council instead permits recurring removal of marram and rhizomes from the road margins, along with routine sand clearance, the direct road and municipal bus will remain open. Residents, care workers, tradespeople, students, and bus passengers will retain current journey times, fares, service frequency, and convenient access to work, education, care, shops, and municipal services. Maintaining the road, however, will preserve a broad, compacted or paved strip with bare safety margins, where heat, unsuitable substrate, lack of shelter, and traffic keep the two dune habitats functionally disconnected. Under the ban, travelers would remain connected to necessities and emergency services through an inland loop, but each trip would take about 30–45 minutes longer, with higher travel costs, reduced bus convenience, and a longer, more weather-exposed walking and cycling route.

Should the municipal council choose the harvest ban and road retirement to restore habitat connectivity, or continued marram removal to protect everyday mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Sand accumulation over the retired carriageway and subsequent marram spread create continuous vegetated dune substrate between the northern and southern habitat areas. Flightless beetles, spiders, and other dune specialists can disperse across the neck without entering an exposed road corridor.
ecologically_protective_option: Adopt a ban on uprooting, cutting, or collecting native marram throughout the dune neck and retire the direct road. Windblown sand would then be allowed to bury the unused carriageway, providing dune substrate through which marram can spread across the former transport corridor.
human_outcome_if_protected: The municipal bus, motorists, and service vehicles must use a safe inland loop that adds approximately 30–45 minutes per trip. Walking and cycling remain possible on a longer surfaced route, but that route is less convenient and more exposed during poor weather. Residents remain connected to necessities and emergency services.
human_protective_option: Authorize recurring removal and collection of marram plants and rhizomes from the carriageway margins and required safety shoulders, together with routine sand clearance, so the direct road and municipal bus can continue operating.
novelty_signature: Active municipal dune neck; native marram harvest ban; windblown sand burying a retired road and supporting revegetation; restored connectivity for flightless dune arthropods; year-round residential district facing a 30–45-minute inland bus and driving loop.
title: Marram-harvest ban on a migrating municipal dune neck

dilemma:
A public desert plateau contains a long-continuous mosaic of centuries-old cushion shrubs, mature hummock grasses, biological soil crusts, undisturbed soil horizons, and connected burrow networks. Its natural runoff patterns support these slowly formed structures, which cannot be recreated on commercial or community-planning time scales. A narrow seam of dimension stone lies beneath the central intact tract. If the public land-management authority withdraws the tract from leasing and prohibits quarry roads, excavation, blasting, spoil placement, and heavy-vehicle use, the old-growth ecosystem and its slow ecological dynamics will remain intact.

The nearby quarry town’s current stone source is nearly exhausted. Its processing sheds require the nearby seam’s particular block size, strength, fracture pattern, and appearance; comparable stone from elsewhere would cost more than the local businesses can absorb. Without a new lease, skilled quarry and cutting jobs will fall sharply, freight and repair demand will contract, and linked shops and service firms will face sustained closures, lower incomes, and unstable municipal revenue. Temporary support can prevent acute deprivation but cannot preserve the town’s production relationships and commercial activity.

Alternatively, the authority can issue a fifteen-year lease and authorize the pit, overburden removal, spoil terraces, haul road, and operating area. This would sustain the town’s principal skilled industry and linked businesses, but excavation would remove the ecosystem within its footprint and fragment adjoining areas through altered runoff, dust, vibration, and traffic. Should the public land-management authority protect the old-growth plateau or protect the town’s local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The ancient shrub–grass–crust mosaic, long-undisturbed soil horizons, connected burrow system, and natural runoff distribution remain intact and continue their slow ecological dynamics without a new industrial break.
ecologically_protective_option: Withdraw the intact plateau tract from mineral leasing and prohibit quarry roads, excavation, blasting, spoil placement, and heavy-vehicle use within it.
human_outcome_if_protected: When the current source closes, the town’s processing sheds lose suitable feedstock. Skilled quarry and cutting employment falls sharply, freight and repair demand contracts, and reduced wages and purchasing lead to sustained closures and income instability among linked local businesses. Temporary income support can prevent acute deprivation but cannot maintain the production relationships and commercial demand that constitute the local stone economy.
human_protective_option: Issue a fifteen-year quarry lease and authorize the pit, overburden removal, spoil terraces, haul road, and operating area required to extract the stone at a commercially viable scale.
novelty_signature: Public desert plateau with centuries-old cushion-shrub, hummock-grass, biological-crust, soil-horizon, and burrow mosaic; proposed shallow dimension-stone lease over a narrow central seam; quarry-town processing cluster dependent on deposit-specific block properties; direct excavation plus disruption of sheet-flow hydrology; minimum pit scale set by road, safety, and equipment investment.
title: Dimension-Stone Lease beneath an Ancient Desert Mosaic

dilemma:
A limestone basin’s spring-fed wetland pools are linked by overflow channels and fast subterranean conduits. Its largest pool is a designated public bathing site and the only free, readily reachable freshwater swimming place in a wide rural district. Without early and repeated applications of a registered copper algaecide, recurring summer cyanobacterial blooms exceed national contact-recreation thresholds. Bathing must then be prohibited during most warm-weather weeks, largely ending regular local swimming, youth water recreation, and long-established summer routines for residents who cannot practically use distant fee-charging alternatives.

The same treatment sends dissolved copper from the bathing pool into smaller connected pools. Copper also binds to fine sediments while remaining available to sensitive organisms. Repeated exposure suppresses sensitive snails, crustaceans, microbial films, and aquatic plants, contaminating the routes and source populations needed for recolonization after seasonal drying and weakening nutrient-cycling processes across the wetland network. A national government, through its pesticide-registration authority, can withdraw authorization for copper algaecide use in hydrologically connected karst wetlands, ending this exposure but requiring the bathing closures. Or it can retain a site-specific authorization for the established treatment schedule, keeping blooms below closure thresholds during most of the summer while copper continues to affect the connected pools. Should the national government withdraw authorization to protect wetland continuity or retain it to protect residents’ recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Copper exposure ends across the linked pools. Sensitive snails, crustaceans, microbial films, and aquatic plants can persist in the smaller pools and disperse through spring outlets and overflow channels, maintaining recolonization after seasonal drying and connected nutrient-cycling processes.
ecologically_protective_option: Withdraw authorization for copper-algaecide use in connected karst wetlands, ending treatment of the bathing pool and the resulting copper exposure throughout this pool network.
human_outcome_if_protected: During most warm-weather weeks, cyanobacterial concentrations exceed national contact-recreation limits and the government-required bathing closure prevents swimming. The surrounding land may remain open for picnicking, but regular local swimming, youth water recreation, and the swimming-centered routines associated with the site largely cease each summer.
human_protective_option: Retain a site-specific authorization for the established early and repeated treatment schedule that keeps cyanobacterial concentrations below contact-recreation closure thresholds during most of the summer.
novelty_signature: Spring-fed karst wetland-pool network; national withdrawal of copper-algaecide authorization; dissolved and sediment-bound copper affects both wetland nodes and subterranean recolonization routes; recurring health-rule closures eliminate a rural district's only practical free freshwater swimming opportunity.
title: Copper-algaecide regulation in interconnected karst pools

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to designate a sheltered island reef complex as a permanent no-take marine protected area. The reef is the region’s principal juvenile habitat for large wrasses and spiny lobsters and includes the deeper reef where adults forage. These predators keep grazing urchins below the density at which kelp recruitment fails. If the agency closes the connected nursery and foraging grounds to commercial take, wrasses and lobsters will recover above that threshold. Kelp beds will persist, sustaining habitat and feeding relationships among producers, invertebrates, reef fishes, and seabirds.

If the agency declines designation, regulated trapping and hook fishing will continue under existing rules. Continued removal will keep predator numbers below the control threshold, allowing urchins to consume new kelp and leaving extensive barrens and a simplified food web. Yet the closure would also remove the only nearby reef that twenty-eight licensed owner-operated boats can reliably work during winter, when offshore grounds are unsafe. Several owners would leave commercial fishing, deckhand jobs would disappear, and the dockside live-seafood buyer would close or operate only seasonally. Transition grants would protect basic needs but would not preserve these fishing occupations or businesses.

Should the state natural-resources agency choose the no-take protected area that preserves trophic integrity or retain fishing access to protect established livelihoods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Wrasses and lobsters recover above the locally measured density needed to suppress grazing urchins. Kelp recruitment and mature kelp cover persist, maintaining habitat and feeding links among producers, invertebrates, reef fishes, and seabirds.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the connected juvenile nursery and adult foraging reef as a permanent no-take marine protected area for wrasses, lobsters, and other harvested reef species.
human_outcome_if_protected: The boats lose their only nearby reef that can be worked reliably in winter. Several owners cease commercial fishing, deckhand positions disappear, remaining operators suffer substantial recurring income losses, and reduced throughput causes the live-seafood buyer to close or become seasonal. Time-limited transition grants protect housing, food, and essential services but do not preserve the fishing occupations, businesses, or buyer network.
human_protective_option: Decline the protected-area designation and retain regulated commercial trapping and hook fishing throughout the reef complex under the existing licensing, gear, reporting, and catch rules.
novelty_signature: Temperate island shelf; connected wrasse-and-lobster nursery and adult foraging reef; locally measured predator threshold controlling urchins; permanent no-take designation to prevent kelp-barren trophic simplification; loss of sheltered winter fishing income, deckhand work, and live-seafood buyer throughput.
title: No-take reserve on a kelp-reef predator nursery

dilemma:
Four municipalities jointly manage a sheltered cove where historic dredging and removed moorings left a broad scar of bare seabed between surviving inner and outer eelgrass beds. The intermunicipal public authority can restore the scarred band by seeding and transplanting native eelgrass, using temporary anchoring grids while it establishes, and permanently prohibiting hauled seines across the restored corridor. The plants would reconnect the beds into a continuous belt of protective feeding structure, allowing juvenile fish, pipefish, small crustaceans, and eelgrass-associated epifauna to move, disperse, and recolonize across the cove under cover rather than crossing exposed sediment.

The same shallow arc and gently shelving beach are the setting for the four towns’ annual communal beach-seine harvest and shore feast. Fishing families, hauling crews, cooks, craftspeople, and residents prepare the net, haul it together, teach younger participants, divide the lawful catch ceremonially, and share the feast. The weighted footrope must sweep the central band to keep fish from escaping; it would uproot eelgrass shoots, cut rhizomes, and reopen the gap. A narrow lane, altered footrope, reseeding after the event, or another shore would not preserve the established practice or the restored corridor. If the authority leaves the sweep bare and renews the permit, the annual haul continues in its customary form, but habitat connectivity remains reduced.

Should the intermunicipal public authority choose eelgrass restoration that protects habitat connectivity or continued beach seining that protects the towns’ cultural practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The restored plants knit the inner and outer beds into a continuous belt of submerged vegetation. Juvenile fish, pipefish, small crustaceans, and eelgrass-associated epifauna can move between the beds while remaining within feeding structure and protective cover, improving exchange and recolonization across the cove.
ecologically_protective_option: Seed and transplant native eelgrass throughout the scarred central band, use temporary low-profile anchoring grids while roots and rhizomes establish, exclude dragging gear during establishment, and permanently prohibit hauled seines across the restored corridor.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents can retain a shore feast or stage a demonstration ashore, but they lose the collective net setting, coordinated hand hauling, catch sharing, gear knowledge, and instruction in the customary cove that together constitute the inherited practice.
human_protective_option: Leave the broad central sweep unvegetated and continue permitting the customary annual beach-seine haul from net setting through coordinated shore hauling and ceremonial distribution of the lawful catch.
novelty_signature: Four-town sheltered cove with dredging and former-mooring scars; active eelgrass transplantation reconnecting inner nursery patches to an outer meadow; functional covered movement for juvenile fish, pipefish, crustaceans, and epifauna; annual cooperative beach-seine ceremony whose widening weighted sweep repeatedly severs the restored rhizome corridor.
title: Eelgrass restoration in a traditional communal-seining cove

dilemma:
A freshwater bay contains the watershed’s last broad native wild-rice stand. Within it, plants associated with wave-washed shallows, sheltered organic coves, and intermediate-depth patches carry distinct genetic variants. Revetments, docks, and a raised access embankment have progressively reduced ice-driven shoreline movement, wave action, and sediment redistribution, shrinking the uncommon margin and cove habitats. If an environmental regulatory agency designates the entire bay and active shoreline as a protected area, it can remove these fixed works and restore the shifting habitat mosaic. The resulting conditions will retain rare alleles and a wider range of traits within the wild-rice population.

Twenty-six lawful year-round homes stand on the narrow shore between the bay and a steep bedrock rise. Their residents depend on their homes, docks, sole access lane, shared winter water system, and close network of kinship and mutual aid. Restoration would make continued safe occupation impractical, requiring the agency to acquire the homes and relocate residents. They would receive full compensation, comparable regional replacement housing, moving expenses, and transition assistance, but no nearby site can keep the households together or preserve their shared system and immediate neighborhood. Alternatively, the agency can exclude the occupied shore, renew permits for defenses and repairs, and allow residents to remain, while the wild-rice stand becomes genetically narrower as its specialized habitats continue to contract.

Should the environmental regulatory agency choose protected-area designation and restoration to protect the wild rice’s genetic diversity, or continued residential permitting to protect residents’ ability to remain in their homes and community?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Renewed shoreline movement recreates and maintains the bay's contrasting shallow-margin, organic-cove, and intermediate-depth habitats. This allows plants associated with all three zones to persist within the same stand and restores opportunities for pollen and seed exchange among them, retaining rare edge- and cove-associated alleles and a wider range of traits.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the whole bay and its active shoreline as a protected area; acquire the twenty-six residences with full compensation; remove revetments, docks, the raised access embankment, and other fixed shoreline works; and restore room for natural ice movement, wave action, and sediment redistribution.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents receive comparable replacement housing within the region, payment for their properties and shares of common infrastructure, moving expenses, and transition assistance. They nevertheless must leave their current homes and disperse among several communities, ending the immediate neighborhood, shared winter-water arrangement, and much routine kin and neighbor support.
human_protective_option: Exclude the occupied shoreline from the protected area and renew permits for revetments, docks, access-lane reinforcement, and necessary ice-damage repairs, allowing residents to remain safely in their existing homes and community.
novelty_signature: Cold freshwater bay with a narrow inhabited shore backed by bedrock; native wild-rice genetic variants associated with wave-washed margins, sheltered organic coves, and intermediate depths; aquatic protected-area restoration of ice, wave, and sediment processes requires removal of armoring and compensated dispersal of a year-round lakeshore community.
title: Ice-scoured lakeshore homes and genetically varied wild rice

dilemma:
A humid mountain plateau’s privately held tea estates lie on steep slopes above a basin of old-growth cloud forest. The forest’s massive uneven-aged trees, acidic organic mats, epiphyte communities, fungi, microfauna, and slow nutrient processes reflect centuries of continuity and cannot be recreated quickly. Persistent copper fungicide applied on the tea fields is carried by heavy rainfall in fine particles and colloids into the basin. The forest’s organic mats retain it, and repeated inputs simplify sensitive fungal and microfaunal communities, slow litter processing, and weaken the regeneration and substrate-forming processes that sustain the old-growth ecosystem.

A regional planning commission can prohibit this fungicide throughout the mapped recharge and runoff area. Doing so would sharply reduce new copper loading and permit a gradual decline in bioavailable copper, supporting eventual recovery of sensitive soil communities and the forest processes they sustain. Yet the wettest contiguous tea blocks depend on the treatment: available substitute fungicides wash off in persistent rain, and untreated disease makes their tea commercially unreliable. Owners and lawful operators would lose recurring production, processing sheds would operate below established throughput, lease income would decline where applicable, and the properties’ dependable agricultural and collateral value would fall, though substantial drier fields, buildings, access, and basic economic security would remain.

Should the regional planning commission prohibit the persistent copper fungicide to protect the old-growth cloud forest, or allow its continued label-compliant use to protect the tea estates’ productive property value?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: New agricultural copper loading into the basin falls sharply. Existing copper does not disappear immediately, but declining inputs allow gradual reduction of bioavailable copper in surface organic layers and eventual recovery of sensitive fungi and microfauna. This preserves the decomposition, mycorrhizal exchange, epiphyte-substrate formation, and uneven-aged regeneration characteristic of the old-growth forest.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit use of the estates' persistent copper fungicide throughout the mapped upslope recharge and runoff area draining into the old-growth basin.
human_outcome_if_protected: Persistent leaf disease makes the wettest contiguous fields commercially unreliable for market-grade tea. Owners lose recurring production from those blocks, processing facilities operate below their established throughput, lease income declines where applicable, and the dependable agricultural and collateral value of the properties falls. Substantial drier fields remain productive, and owners retain their buildings, access, and basic economic security.
human_protective_option: Continue label-compliant copper-fungicide treatment on the existing tea fields, allowing owners and lawful operators to maintain reliable production across the full estates.
novelty_signature: Humid mountain tea plateau draining into a centuries-old cloud forest; regional prohibition of persistent copper fungicide across a mapped runoff source area; cumulative retention in acidic organic mats disrupting fungal, detritivore, epiphyte, and regeneration processes; loss of reliable wet-field production, processing throughput, lease income, and estate value.
title: Fungicide restriction above a relict cloud-forest basin

dilemma:
After household water, sanitation, and dam-safety requirements are met, an elected Indigenous governing council must allocate a fixed dry-season volume from a dam above its coastal settlement. It can spread that water as a continuous low release for five years, maintaining freshwater input to the narrow marine estuary between tides. This would preserve the salinity gradient, limit low-oxygen stratification, keep eelgrass-edge sediments oxygenated, and sustain shellfish filtration, burrowing invertebrates, amphipods, and feeding and refuge habitat for juvenile coastal fish. The flow would be too shallow, however, to cover fixed boulder hazards in the gorge.

Alternatively, the council can retain the established twice-monthly weekend pulses that make local whitewater descents safe. These releases allow volunteer instruction and an affordable, intergenerational recreational practice to continue without ferry travel and overnight accommodation on another island. Yet the long intervals with negligible inflow would leave saline bottom water stratified over organic sediments, depleting oxygen and creating sulfide-rich conditions. Much of the burrowing fauna would be eliminated, eelgrass margins would thin, shellfish function and amphipod production would decline, and the estuary would become a substantially simplified marine community. Brief pulses cannot prevent this damage. Intermediate schedules cannot provide both safe paddling flows and the continuous estuarine threshold.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the continuous release that protects the marine ecosystem or the twice-monthly pulses that protect local recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Continuous inflow maintains the estuary’s salinity gradient, limits persistent bottom-water stratification, keeps eelgrass-edge sediments oxygenated, and sustains shellfish filtration, burrowing invertebrates, amphipod production, and feeding and refuge habitat for juvenile coastal fish.
ecologically_protective_option: Distribute the available discretionary water as a continuous low release for the five-year management period, maintaining freshwater input between tides and preventing prolonged saline stratification in the estuary. This release is too shallow to create a safe paddling window in the gorge.
human_outcome_if_protected: The gorge remains below the discharge needed to cover fixed boulder hazards, so the club suspends local descents and instruction for five years. Regular participants either give up this recurring activity or pay for ferry travel and overnight accommodation to paddle on another island. Other local land- and water-based recreation remains available.
human_protective_option: Store the same discretionary water and discharge it in twice-monthly weekend pulses at the minimum instantaneous flow needed for safe gorge paddling. Only negligible inflow reaches the estuary during the long intervals between pulses.
novelty_signature: Rain-fed Indigenous island river with a boulder gorge and narrow marine estuary; temporal allocation of a fixed dam-release volume between continuous ecological flow and twice-monthly whitewater pulses; prolonged stratification, hypoxia, and eelgrass-edge food-web simplification versus loss of affordable local paddling and instruction.
title: Continuous estuary release or weekend whitewater pulses

dilemma:
A river-basin authority must decide whether to cancel a planned navigation cut and low control weir at a naturally unnavigable boulder rapid. The works would create the depth and bypass passage needed for regular commercial barges serving three former mill towns. Yet the rapid is the entire known range of an endemic grazing snail. Its habitat depends on seasonally variable, turbulent water that keeps boulders free of silt, oxygenates their surfaces, and renews the algal films the snail eats. If the authority cancels the project, this free-flowing regime remains intact and the species retains viable habitat throughout its only range. If it proceeds, backwater from the weir and summer diversion into the cut will reduce velocity and turbulence, leaving sediment on the boulders and eliminating the snail’s sole population.

Cancellation would leave ceramic factories and related firms dependent on steep, capacity-limited roads. Winter closures, truck shortages, and fluctuating fuel costs would continue to disrupt deliveries and shipments, contributing to unstable margins, reduced or irregular shifts, weaker contracts, and less activity for local suppliers and services, though goods and some ceramic production would still continue. Constructing the works would lower and stabilize bulk freight costs, allowing more predictable production schedules and supporting manufacturing, freight work, suppliers, and business turnover across the towns.

Should the river-basin authority cancel the navigation cut and weir to protect the endemic snail, or construct and operate them to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Seasonal changes in velocity and turbulence continue to scour fine sediment, oxygenate exposed rock faces, and renew the attached algal films on which the snail feeds. The species consequently retains viable habitat throughout its only geographic range.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the planned navigation cut and control weir, leaving the boulder rapid's free-flowing hydraulic regime intact.
human_outcome_if_protected: The towns remain dependent on capacity-limited road freight. Weather closures, truck availability, and fuel costs continue to disrupt deliveries and shipments, producing recurring slowdowns, narrower margins, reduced or irregular shifts, weaker order books, and lower demand for local suppliers and services. Essential goods still reach the towns, and some ceramic production continues.
human_protective_option: Construct and operate the navigation cut and low control weir, providing the channel depth and predictable bypass passage required for regular commercial barge service to the three towns.
novelty_signature: Temperate upland boulder rapid; endemic grazing snail dependent on turbulent, silt-free rock and seasonal velocity variation; cancellation of a combined navigation cut and low control weir; backwater inundation plus low-flow diversion versus freight stability for a three-town ceramics manufacturing cluster.
title: Cancel the Kestrel Bend Navigation Cut

dilemma:
A regional government must decide whether to remove a former navigation dam that excludes tides from a broad upper estuary. Complete removal of the dam and its sill would restore daily tidal exchange, saline-water movement, sediment transport, and connection to the lower estuary. Across the basin, differences in elevation and flooding would again support bands of native saltmeadow cordgrass, saltgrass, black-grass, glasswort, sea lavender, and high-marsh shrubs. Without removal, the basin will remain a freshwater impoundment dominated by cattail and wet scrub, and its characteristic zoned salt-marsh plant community will remain absent.

Several family-owned parcels in the low-elevation central basin are lawfully managed as lowbush-blueberry fields. Restored tides would move through their existing ditches and organic soils, repeatedly flooding the fields with brackish water. This would kill the blueberry rhizomes and prevent commercial re-establishment, permanently ending crop or lease income and reducing the land’s agricultural resale and collateral value. The families would retain their homes and upland holdings. Keeping the dam and gates would preserve the freshwater conditions, productive fields, access tracks, and agricultural value on which the owners rely.

Partial opening or diking the fields would not preserve both outcomes: measures that keep the soils fresh would prevent the tidal and salinity conditions needed for the marsh community, while sufficient tidal restoration would salinize the fields. Should the regional government remove the dam to restore the native plant community or retain it to protect the landowners’ property use and value?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Elevation-linked bands of native saltmeadow cordgrass, saltgrass, black-grass, glasswort, sea lavender, and high-marsh shrubs re-form across the basin, restoring the locally characteristic zoned salt-marsh plant community rather than a single-species planting.
ecologically_protective_option: Completely remove the dam and associated sill so that the upper estuary again experiences its surveyed daily tidal range, saline-water exchange, sediment movement, and uninterrupted connection to the lower estuary.
human_outcome_if_protected: Daily brackish flooding kills established blueberry rhizome mats and prevents commercial re-establishment. The parcels permanently lose their established agricultural use, crop or lease income, and a substantial share of their ordinary market and collateral value, although the owners retain their homes and upland property.
human_protective_option: Retain and maintain the dam and gates in their present tide-excluding configuration, preserving the freshwater water table and drainage regime required for continued lowbush-blueberry cultivation.
novelty_signature: Upper coastal estuary converted to freshwater by a regionally owned former navigation dam; complete barrier and sill removal restores elevation-linked salt-marsh plant zonation; tides salinize lawful lowbush-blueberry parcels occupying the basin’s central restoration gradient, eliminating their established agricultural use and substantial property value.
title: Removing a Former Navigation Dam in a Coastal Blueberry District

dilemma:
A state-managed miombo woodland reserve surrounds four rural villages where edible caterpillars emerge densely on mature host trees during each rainy season. Families currently collect and dry them as their cheapest locally available animal protein, relying on stored supplies when roads and market deliveries are unreliable. For low-income households without regular vehicle access, ending collection would mean greater dependence on beans, eggs, dried fish, and similar foods from irregular mobile vendors, raising expenses and creating recurring gaps in affordable protein. Staples and relief foods would still prevent starvation or medically dangerous deprivation.

The public land-management authority can either continue the authorized household harvest or impose a six-year, reserve-wide collection ban. Continued harvesting removes most late-instar caterpillars before peak predation, parasitoid emergence, and frass deposition. Bird, lizard, and small-mammal breeding and recruitment decline; parasitoids become too sparse to maintain their role; and decomposer activity weakens beneath host trees, simplifying the connected canopy-to-soil food web. A ban would leave most caterpillars for predators and parasitoids and maintain frass and remains for decomposers, allowing these trophic relationships to recover and function through variable emergence years. Limited allowances cannot meet both needs, and quotas or spatial rotation cannot be effectively enforced or sustain the required ecological pathways.

Should the public land-management authority impose the harvest ban to protect trophic integrity, or continue household harvesting to protect villagers’ food access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Most of each emergence remains available to insectivorous birds, lizards, small mammals, and parasitoids. Caterpillar frass and uneaten remains continue feeding decomposers and returning canopy nutrients beneath host-tree stands, preserving connected canopy, predator, parasitoid, and soil-detrital pathways.
ecologically_protective_option: Impose a six-year reserve-wide ban on collecting the edible caterpillars. The period covers several caterpillar generations and associated predator and parasitoid breeding cycles, allowing depleted trophic relationships to recover and then remain functional through variable emergence years.
human_outcome_if_protected: Households lose a nearby protein source that can be gathered without cash and stored without dependable transport. They must rely more heavily on beans, eggs, dried fish, or similar foods from irregular mobile vendors, increasing expenditure and causing recurring gaps in affordable protein availability. Basic staples and relief foods continue to prevent starvation or medically dangerous deprivation.
human_protective_option: Continue the currently authorized open household harvest, allowing village families to collect and dry enough caterpillars to remain a meaningful source of affordable food through the lean and transport-disrupted months.
novelty_signature: State-managed miombo reserve; synchronized edible-caterpillar emergence; six-year collection ban; road-isolated villages losing a dried seasonal protein supply; linked canopy-herbivore, bird, lizard, small-mammal, parasitoid, frass, and decomposer pathways.
title: Caterpillar emergence in a miombo reserve

dilemma:
On a cool, treeless island, a nearly continuous blanket bog runs from upland seepages to coastal flushes. Its remaining uncut peat ridges and adjoining recharge areas hold saturated peat at the elevation needed to pass water between bog basins. If these areas are permanently closed to extraction, peat-forming vegetation, linked wet margins, and connected habitat for wetland invertebrates and birds will persist. Older peripheral cuttings can stabilize without new drainage faces advancing into the last hydrological links.

The island environmental regulatory agency can instead renew regulated household peat-cutting licences on those ridges for twenty years. They are the only accessible common plots still containing usable domestic fuel peat; older areas are exhausted, fragmented, or unreachable without new roads. Licensing would let low- and middle-income households continue using low-cost local fuel in existing stoves, comfortably heating their occupied rooms without relying as heavily on weather-delayed imports or costly building conversions. Yet successive cutting, grips, and drainage channels would breach the ridges, lower adjoining water tables, and divide the continuous bog into smaller wet remnants separated by heath, gullies, and bare peat.

A prohibition would end household peat cutting on the island. Imported briquettes or heating oil, a targeted allowance, and an emergency reserve would maintain safe temperatures, but households would spend about 12 percent more of their disposable income on heating, heat fewer rooms in winter, and lose a customary means of providing for themselves. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose permanent protection of the wetland links or renewed licences protecting households’ access to affordable local heating fuel?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The uncut ridges retain their elevation, saturated peat structure, and capacity to pass water between bog basins. Peat-forming vegetation persists, wet margins remain linked from upland seepages to coastal flushes, and wetland invertebrates and birds retain connected habitat and recolonization routes. Existing peripheral cuttings can stabilize and revegetate without new drainage faces advancing into the links.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the remaining connecting ridges and adjoining recharge areas as permanent no-extraction wetland land. Because every remaining accessible common peat plot overlaps this protected area, the designation ends household peat cutting on the island.
human_outcome_if_protected: Affected households replace local peat with imported briquettes or heating oil and heat fewer rooms during winter. A targeted fuel allowance and a regulated emergency reserve ensure that all occupied homes can maintain safe temperatures, but typical affected households still devote about 12 percent more disposable income to heating, face occasional shipment-related conservation periods, and lose a customary form of practical energy self-provisioning.
human_protective_option: Renew regulated household cutting licences on the remaining accessible ridges and recharge areas for twenty years, allowing residents to continue obtaining low-cost local heating fuel with their existing equipment.
novelty_signature: Cool treeless island blanket bog; household peat-cutting licences as a regulated land use; the last accessible fuel plots coincide with narrow saturated ridges and recharge areas linking upland seepages, bog basins, and coastal flushes; extraction ban preserves hydrological and habitat continuity; households shift to imported heating fuel, higher recurring costs, fewer heated rooms, and shipment dependence.
title: Household peat cutting on an island blanket bog

dilemma:
A municipal council must decide the future of a century-old retired hydropower dam in an interior Pacific Northwest valley. The dam maintains a six-kilometre reservoir, but it also attenuates spring floods and traps gravel and large wood upstream. Downstream, an old-growth black cottonwood–western redcedar floodplain depends on seasonal flooding, mobile sediment, large wood, and shifting side channels. Continued impoundment means cottonwood recruitment and side-channel renewal will keep failing; as veteran trees die, the floodplain will lose its uneven-age structure, wet microsites, and disturbance processes. Complete removal of the dam, its sediment-retaining works, flow-control structures, and powerhouse foundation would restore the flood conditions and material movement that sustain this old-growth ecosystem.

For four generations, an Indigenous community has held an annual canoe gathering on the reservoir. Participants travel together from a waterfront longhouse to a burial bluff, teaching canoe handling, songs, protocols, and responsibilities during the calm-water journey and making a collective landing at the bluff. Removal would expose a shallow, boulder-strewn river with two rapids, permanently ending the unified flotilla, ceremonial approach, landing, and route-specific teaching, though both sites would remain accessible by land. Retaining the dam would preserve the gathering in its established form but allow the old-growth floodplain to continue declining.

Should the municipal council remove the dam to protect the old-growth ecosystem or retain it to protect the community’s canoe gathering?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Restored spring floods reconnect and periodically rearrange side channels, deposit fresh alluvium, create bare moist surfaces for cottonwood recruitment, move large wood into the floodplain, and replenish wet microsites. These processes sustain the uneven-age structure and habitat mosaic of the existing old-growth cottonwood–redcedar ecosystem as veteran trees die.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the dam, sediment-retaining structures, flow-control works, and powerhouse foundation to restore an unobstructed channel capable of conveying seasonal flood peaks, gravel, sediment, and large wood to the downstream floodplain.
human_outcome_if_protected: Reservoir drawdown exposes a shallow, boulder-strewn river interrupted by two rapids. The community retains access to the longhouse and burial bluff by existing land routes and can continue other gatherings without displacement or material deprivation, but it permanently loses the unified canoe passage, ceremonial approach and landing, and the intergenerational instruction organized around completing that passage together.
human_protective_option: Retain and maintain the dam and reservoir at the operating range needed to preserve the continuous calm-water canoe route between the longhouse and burial bluff.
novelty_signature: Interior Pacific Northwest old-growth cottonwood–western redcedar floodplain; complete municipal hydropower-dam removal restores spring floods, gravel transport, large wood, side-channel migration, and cottonwood recruitment; an Indigenous community loses a four-generation calm-water canoe gathering linking a longhouse and burial bluff because two rapids re-emerge and prevent a unified ceremonial flotilla.
title: Canoe gathering or restored floodplain forest

dilemma:
In a monsoon river basin, flooded terraced rice fields and gravity-fed ditches form the only wet-season shallow-water connection between two natural marshes. Native climbing perch use this chain of paddies as habitat for movement, breeding exchange, and recolonization after drying. If the river-basin authority prohibits aquatic molluscicide throughout the corridor, the fish can cross the full chain during the monsoon. Wet-season irrigation and flooding will continue under existing tenancy agreements even if rice production declines.

Apple snails, however, consume newly transplanted rice. Without molluscicide, repeated replanting, lower yields, and unreliable receipts will deprive tenant households of a substantial share of their established farm income. Transplanting and harvesting crews will receive far fewer paid days, and the village mill will operate below the level needed for regular staffing. Housing, food support, and transition assistance will prevent severe deprivation, but rice farming and milling will no longer continue at their established occupational scale. Local trials found that untreated stepping-stone paddies allowed snails to recolonize neighboring fields before seedlings became resistant, while screens, hand collection, ducks, and older seedlings did not keep losses below the farms’ viability threshold. Permitting synchronized molluscicide application immediately after transplanting would sustain viable harvests, regular seasonal work, and the mill’s commercial throughput, but several consecutive paddies and connecting ditches would become acutely toxic during the principal fish-movement period, functionally disconnecting the two marsh populations across successive monsoons.

Should the river-basin authority prohibit molluscicide to protect habitat connectivity or permit it to protect established livelihoods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Climbing perch can move through the full flooded paddy chain, allowing dispersal, breeding exchange, and recolonization between the two marshes. Continued wet-season irrigation preserves the physical corridor despite reduced farm profitability.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit the aquatic molluscicide throughout the terraced corridor, leaving the connected paddies and ditches survivable for climbing-perch movement during the monsoon.
human_outcome_if_protected: Apple-snail grazing causes repeated replanting, lower yields, and unreliable farm receipts. Tenant households lose a substantial share of established agricultural income, crews receive markedly fewer paid days, and the village mill operates below the throughput needed for regular staffing. Secure tenancies, temporary income support, and alternative casual work prevent hunger, homelessness, or forced displacement, but do not preserve rice farming and milling at their established occupational scale.
human_protective_option: Permit synchronized molluscicide application immediately after rice transplanting, suppressing apple snails enough to preserve commercially viable harvests and associated field and milling work.
novelty_signature: Monsoon terraced-rice stepping-stone corridor between two natural marshes; apple-snail molluscicide creates a synchronized toxic break for native climbing perch; gravity-fed irrigation and tenancy rules preserve seasonal flooding under either policy; tenant farmers, field crews, and village-mill livelihoods; local trials show that untreated paddies permit rapid snail recolonization.
title: Molluscicide use across a terraced rice corridor

dilemma:
Seven municipalities share a mountain reservoir whose spring allocation determines flows through a broad downstream floodplain. The only low terrace across which water can reach the floodplain’s principal side channels and ponds is occupied by a lawful 34-home riverside hamlet. Its residents include multigenerational households whose gardens, workshop spaces, community hall, and daily networks of informal care are concentrated there.

An intermunicipal public authority can allocate stored water to a six-week annual overbank pulse. The resulting inundation would reconnect the river, side channels, and floodplain ponds, allowing cottonwood and willow recruitment, aquatic-insect production, amphibian breeding, juvenile-fish feeding, and the seasonal transfer of prey to herons, otters, and terrestrial predators. This would maintain a functioning food web across channel and floodplain habitats. But the same releases would inundate yards, the sole access road, wellheads, and septic fields, so the authority would have to acquire the properties and relocate residents beforehand. Replacement-value compensation, suitable homes, and moving support would prevent homelessness, yet the residents would lose their established homes and compact community.

Alternatively, the authority can retain the spring volume for municipal supply and keep releases within the channel. Residents could remain, but the ponds would stay disconnected and stagnate or dry prematurely; food-web functions would substantially decline. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the overbank release that protects trophic integrity or the within-channel allocation that protects residents’ continued residence?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Recurring inundation reconnects the river, side channels, and floodplain ponds. It supports periodic cottonwood and willow recruitment, aquatic-insect production, amphibian breeding, juvenile-fish feeding, and seasonal movement of fish and invertebrate biomass to herons, otters, and terrestrial predators, maintaining a food web that spans channel and floodplain habitats.
ecologically_protective_option: Allocate the required stored spring volume to a six-week overbank pulse each year and, before beginning that release regime, purchase the hamlet's properties at replacement value and relocate residents outside the inundation zone.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents receive replacement-value compensation, suitable replacement homes, and moving support before releases begin, but they are compelled to leave intact lawful homes. The compact hamlet and the proximity supporting gardens, shared facilities, informal care, and multigenerational relationships are lost even if households remain within the wider municipal region.
human_protective_option: Retain the spring volume for municipal supply and limit downstream releases to within-channel flows, allowing residents to remain in their present homes and community.
novelty_signature: Intermunicipal mountain-reservoir allocation between municipal storage and a six-week spring overbank pulse; lawful 34-home hamlet occupying the sole terrace-crossing flow path; reconnection of side channels and ponds supporting riparian producers, insects, amphibians, juvenile fish, herons, otters, and terrestrial predators; recurrent sanitation and access failures requiring advance compensated relocation.
title: Spring flood pulse or continued residence on the Lower Alder floodplain

dilemma:
On a windswept northern archipelago, a national government must decide the future of a state-owned lodgepole-pine fuelwood estate covering the headwaters and central drainage corridor of a lowland watershed. Ending fuelwood rotations would allow the government to remove pine, block plantation drains, selectively remove needle-rich litter where needed, and reseed local heath species. A connected mosaic of dry and wet native heath would return across the watershed, replacing the uniform exotic conifer crop with characteristic plant communities and restored moisture gradients. If harvesting and drainage continue, canopy shade, acidic needles, and pine seed rain will keep the watershed dominated by plantation vegetation, while only small heath remnants remain at its edges.

The estate provides the nonreplaceable majority of the wood chips used by the cooperative district-heating plant serving the main settlement. Continuing rotations would preserve a dependable local fuel supply, stable tariffs, and winter chip reserves for households, a school, food stores, and small workshops. Restoration would require imported compressed biomass and electric backup after temporary clearance material is used, causing persistent tariff increases, smaller winter reserves, and reduced heating of secondary spaces during expensive weeks. Subsidies, tariff support, and minimum-service guarantees would prevent disconnection and dangerous indoor cold, but lower-income residents in old stone buildings and local enterprises would still bear substantial costs. Should the national government choose watershed-scale restoration of the native heath community or continued fuelwood production to protect affordable, reliable heat?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: A connected mosaic of dry and wet native heath returns across the lowland watershed. Characteristic plant composition and moisture gradients replace the uniform exotic conifer crop, including wet-heath communities in the restored drainage corridor and dry-heath assemblages on adjacent rises.
ecologically_protective_option: End fuelwood rotations across the estate, remove mature pine and subsequent regeneration, plug plantation drains, remove needle-rich litter where restoration trials show it is necessary, and reseed locally sourced heather, crowberry, bog-myrtle, native grasses, and wet-heath plants.
human_outcome_if_protected: Heating remains available through imported compressed biomass and added electric backup, supported by a national conversion subsidy and regulated minimum-service guarantee. Even with those safeguards, household tariffs rise persistently, winter fuel reserves become smaller, and workshops and public buildings reduce heating in secondary spaces during the most expensive weeks.
human_protective_option: Continue rotational pine harvesting and drain maintenance across the commercially viable plantation area, preserving the cooperative plant's dependable local chip supply and current heating tariffs but foregoing watershed-scale heath restoration.
novelty_signature: National fuelwood estate on a windswept northern archipelago; removal of exotic pine, drain blocking, selective litter stripping, and local reseeding restore a watershed-scale dry-and-wet native heath mosaic; the main settlement shifts from locally stored woodchips to costlier shipborne biomass and electric backup.
title: Restoring heath on the state fuelwood estate

dilemma:
On three neighboring islands in a subtropical volcanic archipelago, an endemic grazing topshell lives only on wave-cut basalt benches. Adolescents from coastal clans traditionally gather live shells at named family shores for their coming-of-age ceremonies. With elder shell workers, they drill and polish the shells into ceremonial belts, then wear the belts in a public presentation. The practice joins a personal journey, family place, skilled work, oral instruction, and recognition as an adult.

The regional planning commission can either retain cultural permits or impose a twelve-year ban on taking live topshells throughout the shoreline management zones. Permitted collection must use large adults, since smaller shells split during drilling and the established belt already uses the minimum number required. Yet these large shells are the most fecund breeders. Continued annual collection keeps adult density below the fertilization threshold on two islands, suppressing recruitment and larval contribution and leaving the species concentrated on the third island. A ban would allow breeding adults on the depleted islands to recover, restoring recruitment and strengthening the connected population.

Under a ban, ceremonies could continue with inherited belts, replicas, or imported shells, but initiates could not gather and make their own belts from family shores, interrupting the locally specific practice for more than a decade. Should the regional planning commission impose the harvest ban to protect the endemic topshell, or retain cultural permits to protect the established initiation practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Large breeding adults increase above the measured spawning-density threshold on the two depleted islands. Successful fertilization and local recruitment recover there, and those benches again contribute larvae to the connected three-island population, making the endemic species less contracted and more resilient.
ecologically_protective_option: Impose a twelve-year archipelago-wide ban on taking live endemic topshells, including collection under cultural permits.
human_outcome_if_protected: Initiation ceremonies and social recognition can continue using inherited belts, replicas, or imported shells, but initiates cannot complete the customary gathering journey or make a belt from shells collected at their family shores. Elder-led transmission of the locally specific gathering and shell-working practice is interrupted for more than a decade.
human_protective_option: Retain cultural permits allowing each initiate to gather the minimum number of large adult topshells needed for one belt in the established pattern.
novelty_signature: Three-island volcanic archipelago with wave-cut basalt benches; endemic broadcast-spawning grazing topshell; twelve-year live-shell harvest ban; size-selective loss of fecund adults causing density-dependent fertilization failure and reduced larval contribution; coming-of-age belts personally gathered at family shores and crafted with elders.
title: Coming-of-age shell belts and an endemic reef snail

dilemma:
Several established settlements on stable islands along a subarctic river delta are planned to receive a twelve-kilometer all-season gravel road to the regional highway. The approved design requires a raised embankment above spring flood levels, with bridges at major distributaries and culverts across sedge marshes, thaw ponds, minor channels, and areas of diffuse sheet flow. This embankment would block much of the broad overbank flow between crossings. Water would remain longer upstream, while downstream marshes and ponds would receive less water and sediment; faster culvert flows would replace many shallow connections. The roadbed would also persistently divide wetland units, simplifying vegetation patterns and reducing connectivity among aquatic and semi-aquatic populations.

If the regional government cancels the road before tendering, spring floods would continue to spread through the connected mosaic of channels, ponds, and marshes, allowing water, sediment, fish, invertebrates, and semi-aquatic animals to move across the delta margin. Residents would retain ferry service, a winter route when ice permits, and scheduled aircraft, including emergency aviation, but would continue facing high charges, limited baggage and freight capacity, infrequent travel during transition seasons, and no private-vehicle access to the mainland network. Building the road would instead provide year-round vehicle travel for work, appointments, shopping, and family responsibilities.

Should the regional government cancel the road to protect wetland continuity or construct it to protect residents’ mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Spring floods continue spreading through the connected mosaic of distributaries, shallow channels, thaw ponds, and sedge marshes. Water, sediment, fish, aquatic invertebrates, and semi-aquatic animals continue moving across the delta margin, and the timing and duration of seasonal inundation remain coordinated among its wetland units.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the planned all-season road and retain the existing ferry, winter-route, and scheduled-air network, leaving the delta margin physically and hydrologically continuous.
