The cooperative discount grocer would retain its current loading area, but could not expand its truck access or cold storage.

Approving the lease amendment would allow the grocer to pave the terrace for a larger turning and unloading yard and build a refrigerated annex. Consolidated deliveries and immediate cold storage would reduce handling and spoilage costs, supporting lower prices, a broader ordinary food range, and more reliable weekly stocking for residents of three low-income neighborhoods, many of whom lack cars and otherwise need two buses to reach another full-service grocer. Yet the construction would remove the last continuous shaded connection, leaving hot pavement, dry edges, curbs, lighting, and truck traffic that isolate the parks’ cover-dependent populations and make small local populations more vulnerable after ordinary disturbances.

Should the public land-management authority choose the corridor overlay that protects habitat connectivity or approve the expansion that protects affordable, reliable food access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Continuous canopy, moist soil, leaf litter, and understory cover remain between the two parks. Woodland salamanders, ground beetles, small mammals, and understory plant propagules can disperse through the terrace, allowing recolonization and demographic or genetic exchange between habitat areas.
ecologically_protective_option: Adopt a no-build, no-paving, and no-clearing corridor overlay across the full terrace, retain its continuous canopy and understory, and revegetate only compacted terrace margins that are outside the cooperative’s currently authorized loading area.
human_outcome_if_protected: The cooperative remains open and retains its existing authorized loading space, but it cannot accept full shipment-scale deliveries or add adequate cold storage. Suppliers must divide loads, the store misses volume discounts, and pallets sometimes wait for unloading or refrigerated space. Retail prices rise and recurring gaps continue in produce, dairy products, refrigerated foods, and bulk staples.
human_protective_option: Approve the lease amendment and permit the cooperative to pave the terrace for a larger truck-turning and unloading yard and construct the refrigerated annex, allowing shipment-scale deliveries and immediate cold storage.
novelty_signature: Metropolitan river terrace forming the sole shaded terrestrial corridor between woodland parks; public discount-grocery lease expansion; moisture-sensitive salamander, beetle, small-mammal, and plant dispersal; public no-build and no-paving overlay; shipment-scale truck turning and cold-storage capacity determining neighborhood food prices and stock reliability.
title: Riparian corridor or discount-grocery expansion

dilemma:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to cancel a planned replacement gravity-fed slalom course beside a natural rapid in its territory. The existing council-owned course is being dismantled because its diversion wall and training structures no longer meet engineering safety standards. A replacement would provide predictable local whitewater flows for youth teams, adult clubs, families, coaches, school groups, and regional events. Without it, flat-water paddling and occasional trips to a managed course two hours away remain possible, but dependable local instruction, weekly practice, competitions, and family slalom gatherings would end for many participants.

Immediately below the rapid, several connected gravel pockets contain the entire global population of a mussel found nowhere else. If the council cancels the project, seasonal moderate flows will continue to flush fine sediment from these pockets, preserving the pore spaces the mussels need for feeding, respiration, juvenile settlement, and reproduction. If it authorizes the course, its low diversion sill and side-channel intake will reduce the velocity and bed shear of those same flows below the threshold needed to clear sediment. The gravel will repeatedly become embedded, impairing adults and preventing juvenile recruitment throughout the species’ last habitat, placing it on a trajectory toward global loss.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council cancel the replacement course to protect the endemic mussel, or build and operate it to preserve affordable, predictable local whitewater recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Seasonal moderate-flow events continue to pass through the natural rapid with enough velocity and bed shear to remove accumulated fine sediment from all remaining mussel gravel pockets. Open pore spaces preserve adult feeding and respiration, juvenile settlement, and reproduction across the endemic species’ entire global range.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the replacement slalom course, remove temporary project works, and leave the natural rapid and downstream reach without a new sill, intake, or training-flow diversion.
human_outcome_if_protected: Flat-water paddling and occasional trips to distant courses remain possible, but dependable local whitewater instruction, weekly club practice, youth progression, competitions, and family-centered slalom gatherings end. Travel cost and time prevent many younger participants and families from using the distant course regularly.
human_protective_option: Build and operate the replacement gravity-fed slalom course using a low diversion sill, side-channel intake, and fixed control structures that provide predictable training flows throughout the paddling season.
novelty_signature: Indigenous-governed bedrock rapid; globally endemic gravel-pocket mussel; cancellation of an unsafe slalom course’s gravity-fed replacement; sill backwater and training-flow diversion suppress measured sediment-cleansing shear; youth teams, families, and paddling clubs lose dependable local whitewater recreation.
title: Cancel a replacement whitewater course to preserve an endemic river mussel

dilemma:
Across a cool-temperate estuary, naturally floating sedge marshes link an inland fen to shallow lagoons and the sea. Their living sedges and interwoven rhizomes form buoyant mats through which water, seeds, organic matter, invertebrates, amphibians, and other wetland organisms move. Licensed crews cut and roll sections of these mats for erosion-control products at a worker-owned cooperative mill in the principal town. At the minimum harvest volume needed to keep the mill open, the resulting openings align with winter waves. Unsupported edges tear, nearby gaps merge, and detached rafts strand or sink, progressively dividing the wetland chain into isolated remnants.

Under national wetland law, a national government may ban commercial removal of live sedge mats throughout the estuary for twelve years. This would allow cut edges to knit together, restore continuity across old openings, and preserve the connected functioning of the marshes. But without legal live-mat supply, the mill would close; cutting, processing, haulage, repair, dock, and storage income would disappear, buyers would turn elsewhere, and the town would lose a reliable specialized employment network for many years. Social insurance and casual work remain available, but predictable seasonal income for the cooperative and linked businesses would decline.

Should the national government choose the twelve-year harvest ban that protects wetland continuity, or continue permits at the minimum annual volume that protects local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Continuous living rhizome mats remain buoyant, recover across old openings, and maintain linked wetland habitat from the inland fen through the lagoons to the estuary. Water, seeds, organic matter, invertebrates, amphibians, and other wetland organisms can continue moving among the component marshes.
ecologically_protective_option: Ban commercial removal of live sedge mats throughout the estuary for twelve years, allowing cut edges to knit together and the floating marsh chain to expand across existing gaps.
human_outcome_if_protected: With no legal supply of live sedge mat, the cooperative mill falls below operating scale and closes. Cutting, processing, haulage, repair, dock, and storage income disappear, and established buyers shift to other suppliers. Workers remain housed and eligible for social insurance and available casual employment, but the town loses a reliable specialized employment and business network for many years.
human_protective_option: Continue issuing permits for the minimum annual harvest volume needed to keep the cooperative mill operating, retain its trained workforce, and fulfill recurring buyer contracts.
novelty_signature: Cool-temperate estuarine chain of floating sedge marshes; commercial removal of living rhizome-bound rolls for erosion-control products; cut openings increase winter-wave fetch and cause mat tearing, stranding, and sinking; twelve-year national harvest ban versus the operating scale and buyer continuity of a worker-owned mill and its town-wide service network.
title: Floating-Marsh Sedge Harvest Ban

dilemma:
A municipal council must decide whether to remove an obsolete irrigation dam whose crest carries the narrow public road linking two orchard villages to the valley service center and regional transport. Complete removal would drain the reservoir and restore diffuse spring flow, shallow groundwater variation, and natural salinity gradients across the valley floor. Rush meadow, saltgrass flats, greasewood margins, and seasonal wildflowers could again form a connected native plant community, with its zones able to shift as wetting patterns change. Retaining and rehabilitating the dam would leave the central habitat under deep, stable impoundment, with weeds along the reservoir edge and only narrow native fragments.

Removing the dam would also close the crest road. Residents would still reach schools, medical care, jobs, shops, emergency services, and regional transport, but the only all-season public route would add 29 kilometers and about 45 minutes each way. School and worker minibuses would make fewer daily rotations, and some early or evening trips would no longer connect with regional buses. Households would face recurring additional fuel or fare costs. Keeping the dam would preserve the direct twelve-minute route and its timed minibus connections, but would continue to prevent recovery of the valley’s native plant community.

Should the municipal council choose complete dam removal to protect the native plant community, or rehabilitate and retain the dam to protect residents’ mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Across the former reservoir floor, dispersed spring flow, shallow groundwater variation, and natural soil-salinity gradients support a connected mosaic of rush meadow, saltgrass flats, greasewood margins, and native seasonal wildflowers. The component zones remain adjacent and can shift locally as spring discharge and wetting patterns vary.
ecologically_protective_option: Completely remove the dam, spillway, and crest-road embankment; use staged drawdown to avoid burying the spring outlets; regrade only compacted construction surfaces; control reservoir-edge weeds; and use seed collected from local remnant and reference stands where natural recolonization is insufficient. The restored floor would then remain free of a replacement road so diffuse spring flow and the full wet-meadow-to-alkali-shrub zonation can recover.
human_outcome_if_protected: Travel to the valley service center shifts to the only other public road, which circles a bedrock ridge and adds 29 kilometers and about 45 minutes each way. Longer cycles force the school and worker minibuses to reduce daily rotations, and some early or evening trips no longer connect with the fixed regional-bus timetable. Households also incur recurring additional fuel or fare costs. The villages retain road access, emergency response, and access to all essential destinations, and no household must relocate.
human_protective_option: Rehabilitate and retain the dam and its crest road, preserving the villages’ direct, all-season route to valley services and regional transport.
novelty_signature: Dry intermontane spring valley; obsolete municipal irrigation-dam crest serving as the direct road for two orchard villages; complete removal restores a connected rush-meadow–saltgrass–greasewood–wildflower community through diffuse spring flow and salinity zonation; the only nonintrusive road alternative is a 29-kilometer upland detour that lengthens trips and reduces school and worker minibus rotations.
title: Reservoir causeway linking orchard villages to the valley bus line

dilemma:
Four municipalities share a volcanic caldera where warm springs, supplied by a confined geothermal reservoir, sustain a mineral wetland. The springs support warm microbial mats and other primary producers, grazing snails and insect larvae, small native fish, amphibians, and resident and wintering birds that feed on wetland prey. Existing geothermal wells also supply a jointly owned district-heating network used by about 8,000 apartment residents and small shops. Four approved production wells would provide enough local heat to meet winter peak demand while maintaining current tariffs, ordinary overnight temperatures, and unrestricted hot-water service.

Pressure tests show that operating the new wells for useful winter capacity would lower reservoir pressure below the threshold that sustains every spring. Two peripheral springs would stop flowing, while remaining warm reaches would shrink. Primary-production zones and their associated prey would decline, weakening feeding links for fish and amphibians and reducing bird foraging opportunities.

The intermunicipal public authority can designate the entire recharge basin as a protected area, barring the wells and holding current withdrawals at their capped level. Essential heat and hot water would remain available, but tariffs would rise, overnight network settings would be cooler, and nonessential hot-water use would face scheduled limits during the coldest weeks. Should the intermunicipal public authority designate the protected area to preserve trophic integrity or allow the wells to protect affordable, unrestricted winter energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Reservoir pressure remains above the measured spring-flow threshold. All warm springs continue discharging, preserving warm microbial mats and other primary producers, grazing snails and insect larvae, small native fish, amphibians, and the resident and wintering birds that feed on wetland prey.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the entire mapped spring recharge basin as a protected area, prohibit the four new production wells and any other increase in geothermal withdrawal within the shared pressure compartment, and continue existing withdrawals at their current capped level.
human_outcome_if_protected: Existing geothermal output supplies the base heating load, while electric boilers cover part of winter demand. Because peak electricity is costly and boiler capacity cannot support unrestricted simultaneous demand, the utility raises tariffs, adopts cooler overnight network settings, and schedules limits on nonessential hot-water use during the coldest weeks. A hardship tariff and legally required minimum indoor temperatures remain in force.
human_protective_option: Decline protected-area designation for the recharge basin, drill and connect the four approved production wells, and use their output to meet winter peak heating demand at current tariffs without scheduled household hot-water or temperature restrictions.
novelty_signature: Intermunicipal volcanic caldera with an existing geothermal district-heating utility; protected designation of a confined spring recharge basin; measured pressure threshold linking added wells to warm-spring loss; microbial mats and invertebrates supporting fish, amphibians, and birds; essential heat retained but tariffs, overnight settings, and hot-water access constrained.
title: Caldera wetland reserve versus expansion of a geothermal heating field

dilemma:
A subtropical river basin’s old-growth blackwater swamp forest contains veteran hollow trees, deep organic soils, accumulated deadwood, and long-established fungal and invertebrate communities. Fern farms on surrounding former swamp land operate lawfully under expiring authority leases, but their connected drains and shared outfall lower the dry-season water table along the forest’s edge. If drainage continues, exposed organic soil will keep oxidizing and subsiding, veteran trees will face repeated root stress, and dry-site species and predators will progressively displace characteristic swamp organisms from the perimeter inward.

The river-basin authority can decline to renew the leases, close the outfall, block drains, remove raised production beds, and restore a continuous swamp buffer. This would retain water, reduce damage at the old-growth margin, and allow swamp vegetation, organic-soil processes, and specialist communities to recover across the strips. It would also end commercial fern production there. Although compensation, debt settlement for eligible improvements, temporary income support, and retraining would prevent severe deprivation, growers would lose established businesses, and cutters, graders, and refrigerated-truck contractors would have to seek lower-paid or less regular work after the shared grading and transport system becomes unviable.

Alternatively, the authority can renew the leases and preserve the year-round production, floral-market contracts, grading shed, collection route, and specialized livelihoods, while leaving the forest’s edge subject to continued drawdown. Should the river-basin authority choose full restoration to protect the old-growth ecosystem or renew the leases to protect these livelihoods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Closing the outfall and blocking the drains removes the artificial hydraulic gradient around the old-growth edge. The restored strips retain wet-season water and slow dry-season drawdown, reducing peat oxidation, soil subsidence, root stress, and penetration by dry-site species and predators. As swamp vegetation and organic-soil processes recover, the buffer also provides habitat through which characteristic fungi, invertebrates, and plants can disperse when old trees fall and canopy gaps shift.
ecologically_protective_option: Decline renewal of the fern-farm leases, compensate documented leasehold improvements and transition costs, close the shared drainage outfall, block field drains, grade down raised production beds, and establish locally sourced swamp trees and appropriate ground-layer vegetation as a continuous wet buffer around the old-growth core.
human_outcome_if_protected: Compensation pays for documented improvements, unresolved equipment obligations, and transition costs, while temporary income support and retraining prevent destitution. Even with that assistance, rewetting ends commercial fern production on the leased strips. Output falls below the volume needed to support the shared grading shed and scheduled refrigerated collection route, so growers lose established businesses and most cutters, graders, and transport contractors must seek lower-paid or less regular work in the documented regional farm and warehouse labor market.
human_protective_option: Renew the agricultural leases and continue the pumping, drainage, raised beds, and vehicle access required for commercial fern production, while limiting habitat work to unused corners that do not alter the operating drainage regime.
novelty_signature: Subtropical old-growth blackwater swamp buffered by authority-leased ornamental-fern strips; closure of a shared drainage outfall, drain blocking, and raised-bed removal reverse peat-mediated edge drawdown; restoration protects veteran trees and specialist soil communities while ending a volume-dependent grading and refrigerated-transport livelihood cluster.
title: Rewetting Plantation Strips Around an Ancient Swamp Forest

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
A state or provincial natural-resources agency operates a headwater reservoir that supplies a permitted early-winter snowmaking diversion to a privately owned ski area and releases water to an alpine stream inhabited by native sculpin. Upstream and downstream breeding groups carry different cold-metabolism and disease-resistance variants. During recurring low-inflow periods, the fish can move between winter refuges and contribute to breeding only if reservoir releases keep shallow riffles above a measured under-ice depth threshold. Reserving enough water for continuous passage would maintain gene flow and reduce the loss of these distinct variants through drift and inbreeding.

That reservation would reduce the ski area’s historical snowmaking allocation during its narrow early freezing window. It would leave insufficient water to establish a durable base on much of the developed lower-elevation terrain, causing delayed or intermittent closures and reducing lift revenue, concession rent, equipment use, and the income and resale value tied to its lifts, graded runs, pipelines, pumps, and snowmaking plant. The resort could still operate higher natural-snow terrain. Granting the historical allocation, however, would preserve ordinary use and value of those specialized facilities while allowing the riffles to become repeatedly impassable, isolating the smaller upstream group and making its rare variants progressively more likely to disappear, even though the species would remain in the watershed. Should the agency reserve water for winter stream connectivity or allocate it to protect the ski area’s property use?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The riffles remain passable beneath the ice, allowing sculpin from both breeding groups to reach the other group’s winter refuges and contribute to breeding. This recurring gene flow maintains representation of the documented cold-metabolism and disease-resistance variants across the population.
ecologically_protective_option: Reserve enough stored water for continuous winter stream discharge above the measured riffle-connectivity threshold, reducing the ski area’s early-winter snowmaking allocation.
human_outcome_if_protected: Snowmaking volume is insufficient during the early freezing window to establish a durable base on much of the developed lower-elevation terrain. Those runs open late or remain intermittently closed, reducing holiday and early-season lift revenue, concession rent, equipment use, and the income and resale value attributable to the snowmaking-dependent improvements. The resort remains operable on its higher natural-snow terrain.
human_protective_option: Grant the ski area its historical early-winter snowmaking allocation, allowing stream discharge to fall below the connectivity threshold during freeze-up and subsequent low-inflow intervals.
novelty_signature: Alpine ski property supplied by a state headwater reservoir; winter allocation between measured under-ice sculpin connectivity and early-season snowmaking; cold-metabolism and disease-resistance variants maintained through monitored breeding exchange; recurring impairment of lifts, graded runs, pipelines, pumps, concessions, and other snowmaking-dependent property.
title: Winter headwater flow versus snowmaking property use

dilemma:
A reservoir-regulated river narrows between reed shelves that become too shallow for large fish during scheduled drawdowns. Twenty-seven lawfully licensed houseboats, occupied as primary homes, stand in two offset rows across most of the only channel that remains adequately deep year-round. Their piles, cross-channel utility lines, illuminated gangways, and routine maneuvering leave migratory eels, lampreys, and barbel with only narrow, brightly lit passages. As a result, movement between downstream feeding and overwintering habitat and upstream spawning or maturation reaches remains too low to prevent demographic isolation.

The houseboats also form a settled neighborhood. Residents share childcare, meals, repairs, transport, and daily assistance for older people. The river-basin authority may designate the narrows as a protected aquatic migration corridor, remove the infrastructure, and relocate every vessel to licensed downstream basins. This would restore a continuous, dark, deep route for fish, but would compel all households to leave their present homes. Although the authority would provide replacement berths and pay relocation-related costs, no single basin can hold all twenty-seven vessels, so the community would be divided among three sites.

Alternatively, the authority can exclude the narrows from protection and renew the mooring licences, allowing residents to remain in their homes and preserve their community, while the only year-round deep migration route remains obstructed. Should the river-basin authority designate the protected corridor or renew the licences to protect the residents’ continued homes and community?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Removal of the mooring infrastructure creates a continuous, dark, adequately deep route through the narrows. Locally monitored migratory eels, lampreys, and barbel can again move reliably between downstream feeding and overwintering habitat and upstream spawning or maturation reaches during their seasonal movement windows.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the narrows as a protected aquatic migration corridor, prohibit permanent residential moorings and fixed cross-channel utilities within it, remove the piles and chains, extinguish the mooring-field lighting, and relocate the houseboats to licensed downstream basins.
human_outcome_if_protected: Every household retains its vessel and receives a lawful replacement berth, but all are compelled to move their primary homes from the present site. Because no approved basin has capacity for all twenty-seven vessels, the community is divided among three basins, weakening daily mutual-aid arrangements and increasing travel to schools, work, and established neighbors.
human_protective_option: Exclude the narrows from the protected area and renew the residential mooring licences, allowing all households to keep their primary homes at their current berths and preserve the compact floating community.
novelty_signature: Reservoir-regulated river narrows occupied by a licensed permanent houseboat neighborhood; offset mooring rows, piles, submerged utilities, safety lighting, and drawdown-exposed reed shelves constrict the sole year-round deep fish-migration route; aquatic protected-area designation preserves the vessels as homes but compels their dispersal among three replacement basins.
title: Relocating a houseboat community from a deep migration channel

dilemma:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to remove the concrete diversion weir serving its community’s run-of-river power plant. The Pali stream goby exists nowhere beyond the island’s eastern watershed. Its juveniles must climb from the estuary to cool upper tributaries, but the weir’s smooth face and concrete apron block most of them, while diversion dries the bypassed reach’s climbing margins during migration. If the council removes the weir, intake apron, and armoring, a continuously wetted rough channel will reconnect the estuary to all three upper tributaries. The goby’s breeding groups will again exchange individuals across most of its range. If the weir remains, two upper breeding groups will disappear locally, leaving the species confined to one warmer, more disturbed lower-stream area.

The plant supplies about one-third of the electricity used by 1,300 residents and several family workshops. Removing the weir ends that generation. Imported-diesel backup will preserve clinic service, basic lighting and cooking, minimum refrigeration, and enough power to avoid dangerous deprivation, but tariffs will rise persistently. Residents will face scheduled nonessential evening curtailments, workshops will shorten shifts, and communal cold storage will be available only in assigned time slots. Retaining the weir preserves current tariffs, ordinary evening electricity, unrestricted refrigeration schedules, and workshop hours.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council remove the weir to protect the endemic Pali stream goby or retain it to protect the community’s affordable, reliable energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Removal restores a continuously wetted, rough channel from the estuary to all three cool upper tributaries. Returning juveniles can reach the upper breeding areas, and the three breeding groups can again exchange individuals across most of the endemic species’ watershed range.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the diversion weir, intake apron, and armoring along the bypassed reach, then stabilize the disturbed banks without installing another channel-spanning barrier.
human_outcome_if_protected: Diesel backup and protected circuits preserve clinic service, basic household lighting and cooking, minimum refrigeration, and enough power to avoid dangerous deprivation. Nevertheless, households pay persistently higher tariffs and experience scheduled nonessential evening curtailments. Family workshops shorten shifts, and users of communal cold storage must operate within assigned time slots.
human_protective_option: Retain and continue operating the existing weir and run-of-river plant, preserving its present affordable output and evening generating capacity.
novelty_signature: Self-governing tropical Indigenous island; watershed-endemic amphidromous climbing goby; removal of a run-of-river intake weir and apron restores wetted migration margins; council-owned microgrid loses one-third of its supply; imported diesel preserves essential service but causes evening curtailments, higher tariffs, and reduced workshop and communal-refrigeration access.
title: Removing the Intake Weir for the Pali Stream Goby

dilemma:
Four municipalities share a warm limestone coast where submerged caves, entrances, and shaded ledges form a connected marine district. Licensed divers lawfully collect natural sponges under concessions issued by the intermunicipal marine-commons authority. The largest, slow-growing sponge colonies filter water, process nutrients, and create cavities and irregular refuge for crustaceans, juvenile groupers, worms, and colonial invertebrates. Because harvest has removed large marketable colonies faster than comparable colonies can mature, cleared walls remain dominated by short-lived mats and small recruits. Filtration and structural refuge remain depressed, and cave-community assemblages are sparse and fragmented across connected entrances and ledges.

Five years of monitoring under successively reduced quotas showed that any commercially meaningful harvest remained concentrated on the same mature colonies, with removals still exceeding their replacement, while rotating entrances allowed reopened sectors to be harvested before mature structure and connectivity returned. The authority can therefore either impose a fourteen-year ban on commercial and personal sponge harvest throughout the district or continue licensed cutting under the current quota. A ban would allow large colonies to survive through multiple maturation and recruitment cycles, reconnecting habitat and supporting a more complex marine community. It would also leave the cooperative of licensed divers with no legal crop from its concessions for fourteen years. Their purpose-built curing house would lose its ordinary function, and their specialized boats, compressors, concessions, supplemental income, and retirement assets would lose substantial value, although compensation and other income protect housing and basic needs. Continuing the quota would preserve the productive use, transfer value, and seasonal returns of those lawful holdings, while mature sponge habitat, filtration, and refuge would remain reduced. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the fourteen-year harvest ban to protect the marine ecosystem or continue licensed harvesting to protect the cooperative’s property interests?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Large sponge colonies survive through multiple maturation cycles, reconnecting three-dimensional habitat along cave entrances and shaded ledges. Their filtration, nutrient processing, and refuge structure support a more complex and spatially connected cave-community assemblage.
ecologically_protective_option: Ban commercial and personal sponge harvest throughout the submerged-cave district for fourteen years, allowing several uninterrupted growth and recruitment cycles.
human_outcome_if_protected: The concessions produce no legal crop for fourteen years, the site-specific curing house loses its ordinary function, and the boats and compressors lose much of their specialized value. Members forgo supplemental income and experience a substantial reduction in concession and retirement-asset value, although transition compensation and their other incomes protect housing and basic needs.
human_protective_option: Continue licensed sponge cutting under the current quota, preserving the productive use and transfer value of the concessions, boats, equipment, and curing house.
novelty_signature: Warm limestone submerged-cave district; transferable natural-sponge concessions linked to a waterfront curing house; selective removal of slow-growing filter-feeding habitat formers at cave entrances; fourteen-year intermunicipal harvest ban versus productive concession use, specialized property, and retirement-asset value.
title: Sponge-harvest closure in a submerged cave district

dilemma:
During a forecast two-season locust outbreak in a semi-arid inland district, bands move repeatedly between rain-fed millet fields and openings in a large, long-continuous dry forest. The regional environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to deny broad-spectrum aerial spraying across the field–forest mosaic, including forest edges and internal openings. That choice would prevent spray deposition and drift into the old-growth ecosystem, preserving seasonal insect abundance and the pollination, decomposition, aquatic emergence, prey, and nutrient-transfer relationships that connect ancient trees, deadwood, termite mounds, seasonal pools, birds, bats, and reptiles.

Without synchronized aerial treatment across the full outbreak area, locusts sheltering in forest openings will return to adjacent millet during grain filling. Two consecutive saleable harvests will be substantially reduced, along with retained seed and household grain reserves. Trucked maize and other grains will prevent acute hunger, but limited transport and storage capacity will leave low-income households in six market towns facing elevated meal prices, recurring shop stock gaps, less dietary variety, and pressure on ordinary household and school food budgets. A partial campaign would still expose forest margins to drift while failing to protect enough millet for local mills and markets.

Should the environmental regulatory agency choose to protect the old-growth ecosystem or to protect reliable, affordable food access for the six towns?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The old-growth dry forest retains its seasonal insect abundance and the associated pollination, decomposition, aquatic emergence, prey, and nutrient-transfer relationships linking canopy, deadwood, termite mounds, seasonal pools, birds, bats, and reptiles.
ecologically_protective_option: Deny authorization for broad-spectrum aerial locust spraying across the field–forest mosaic, including forest edges and internal openings, thereby preventing direct spray deposition and drift into the old-growth ecosystem.
human_outcome_if_protected: Locust feeding substantially reduces two consecutive saleable millet harvests and consumes part of the retained seed and household grain reserve. Trucked substitutes prevent acute hunger, but local meal prices remain elevated, village shops experience recurring stock gaps, and low-income households reduce food variety and other ordinary purchases.
human_protective_option: Authorize repeated, synchronized aerial treatment across the full outbreak area during the two affected growing seasons, including bands occupying forest openings, to keep locust numbers below the level that would substantially reduce the district’s millet supply.
novelty_signature: Ancient semi-arid dry-forest and millet-field mosaic; emergency regulation of synchronized aerial locust treatment; mobile bands repeatedly using rocky forest openings as treatment refuges; spray exposure coinciding with terrestrial and seasonal-pool insect emergence; old-growth pollination, decomposition, prey, and nutrient pathways versus a two-harvest staple-price and stock-reliability burden across six towns.
title: Locust-control restriction around an ancient dry-forest mosaic

dilemma:
On a windy oceanic headland, separate cliff colonies of wild perennial brassica carry distinct combinations of flowering-time, salt-spray-tolerance, and drought-response variants. Nearby farms have lawfully grown commercial flowering brassica seed, but bees carry crop pollen across the measured four-kilometre range. Repeated hybridization and backcrossing introduce the same abundant commercial alleles into every colony. If this continues, the wild plants will remain, yet rare local variants and the genetic differences among the cliff lineages will progressively decline.

A regional planning commission can adopt a continuing overlay that prohibits commercial flowering brassica seed crops within four kilometres of each wild colony, while allowing unrelated crops and brassicas harvested before flowering. This would reduce crop-pollen input enough for the colonies to retain their distinctive genetic variation. But the three seed-growing households would lose premium seed contracts, seasonal field positions would disappear, and the cleaning and certification cooperative would fall below the volume needed to cover its costs. The households could keep their land, grow lower-margin crops, and receive conversion grants, but their specialist income would decline markedly and the established cooperative operation would become nonviable.

If the commission declines the restriction, the farms’ contracted rotations, specialist work, seasonal employment, certification throughput, and associated income will continue, while the headland’s wild lineages become increasingly genetically homogenized. Should the regional planning commission adopt the ecologically protective overlay or preserve the established seed-growing livelihood?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Crop-pollen input falls below the level causing recurrent introgression, allowing each cliff colony to retain its distinctive combinations of flowering-time, salt-spray-tolerance, and drought-response variants.
ecologically_protective_option: Adopt a continuing agricultural-use overlay prohibiting commercial flowering brassica seed crops within four kilometres of every wild colony. Unrelated crops and brassicas harvested before flowering remain permitted.
human_outcome_if_protected: The farms lose their premium brassica-seed contracts, and the cooperative falls below the cleaning volume needed to cover certification costs. The households retain their land and can grow lower-margin crops with conversion grants, but specialist farm income declines markedly, seasonal positions are lost, and the established cleaning and certification operation becomes nonviable.
human_protective_option: Decline the crop-category restriction and allow the farms to continue their established contracted brassica-seed rotations under existing land-use permissions.
novelty_signature: Oceanic cliff colonies of wild perennial brassica; four-kilometre agricultural-use overlay against flowering commercial seed crops; bee-mediated introgression of shared crop alleles; loss of flowering-time, salt-spray, and drought-response lineage differences; specialist seed-farm and certification-cooperative income decline.
title: Flowering-crop buffer around wild coastal brassicas

dilemma:
A public land-management authority must decide whether to cancel a planned concrete-lined flood-bypass channel and maintenance road across a desert conservation estate. The channel’s only hydraulically workable alignment crosses the estate’s sole broad remnant of a native alluvial-fan plant community: a contiguous mosaic of saltbush, bursage, native grasses, and ephemeral wildflowers. If the project is cancelled, diffuse fan flows will continue to shift among distributaries, sorting sediment, redistributing seeds, and creating the changing moisture conditions that sustain this plant community. If it is built, it will permanently capture principal distributary flows, dry downslope patches, concentrate scour and deposition along its margins, and divide the community with a channel, road, and persistent invasive-plant edges.

The bypass would also keep recurring shallow fan flows out of a forty-home village, preserving residents’ homes, long-held plots, shared courtyards, nearby relatives, and neighborhood continuity. Without it, the authority must acquire the parcels before the safety-compliance deadline, relocate households to comparable serviced homes in the adjacent town, provide compensation and moving assistance, and remove the village infrastructure. Residents would be safe and housed, but would be compelled to leave their established community. Smaller structures, alternative routes, and household floodproofing cannot meet the required safety standard while keeping the village’s shared road, drainage, and septic system functional.

Should the public land-management authority cancel the bypass to protect the native plant community, or construct it to protect residents’ ability to remain in their homes?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Diffuse runoff can shift among distributaries, sort and deposit sediment, redistribute seeds, and create changing moisture conditions across the lower fan. These processes sustain the contiguous native mosaic of shrub patches, grass bands, and ephemeral-wildflower openings.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the bypass channel and maintenance road, acquire the village parcels, relocate residents before the safety-compliance deadline, remove the acquired buildings and residential infrastructure, and restore disturbed ground so diffuse fan flows can again cross the lower fan.
human_outcome_if_protected: Households are relocated safely and receive comparable serviced housing, purchase or lease-value compensation, and moving costs. They nevertheless must leave their present homes, inherited or long-held plots, shared spaces, nearby relatives, and established neighborhood relationships.
human_protective_option: Construct and maintain the full bypass channel and road, intercepting routine fan flows so residents can remain in their present homes and neighborhood.
novelty_signature: Active desert alluvial fan supporting a saltbush–bursage–native-grass–ephemeral-wildflower mosaic; cancellation of a concrete flood-bypass channel and maintenance road; shifting distributaries and sediment sorting maintain the plant community; shared-road and collective-septic compliance requires compensated relocation of a forty-home village.
title: Cancel the flood-bypass channel or retain homes in an alluvial-fan village

dilemma:
A regional electric railway crosses a basalt ridge through an aging tunnel beneath a perched aquifer. For the next eight years, the regional government must decide whether to reserve the aquifer’s limited dry-season yield for the wooded valley’s spring runs or renew pumping that keeps the tunnel safe for normal rail service. Reserving the water would maintain continuous flow, oxygenated riffles, and connected pools. Periphyton and leaf litter would sustain grazing and shredding insects; those insects would support minnows and salamanders, and aquatic insects and vertebrate prey would sustain kingfishers, water snakes, and other riparian predators. Pumping at the established rate would intercept most dry-season recharge, causing several spring runs to stop flowing and weakening these food-web relationships.

Without dewatering, hydrostatic pressure would exceed the tunnel lining’s certified limit, requiring its closure. Safe replacement buses would still connect the three outer suburbs to work, education, medical appointments, caregiving, and family visits, but the winding ridge-road trips would add 45–70 minutes each way, run less often in the evening, require additional transfers, and lack train capacity during peak periods. Renewing pumping would preserve frequent through-trains, affordable predictable travel times, and convenient connections, particularly for households without routine access to a car. Pumping below the operational rate would still leave tunnel pressure above the certified limit while withdrawing enough water to stop flow in the smallest spring runs.

Should the regional government reserve the aquifer for the spring-run food web or renew tunnel pumping to protect residents’ mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Continuous spring flow preserves oxygenated riffles and connected pools. Periphyton and retained leaf litter support grazers and shredders; abundant aquatic insects support native minnows and salamanders; and those organisms sustain kingfishers, water snakes, and other riparian predators.
ecologically_protective_option: End the tunnel's groundwater-withdrawal permit for the eight-year allocation period and reserve the perched aquifer's dry-season yield for continuous discharge through the valley spring runs.
human_outcome_if_protected: Hydrostatic pressure rises above the existing tunnel lining's certified limit, requiring closure throughout the eight-year allocation period. Safe replacement buses remain available on a winding ridge road, but they add 45–70 minutes per one-way trip, run less frequently in the evening, involve additional transfers, and cannot match train capacity during peak periods.
human_protective_option: Renew tunnel pumping at the established dry-season rate, keeping groundwater pressure below the existing lining's certified safety limit and allowing normal through-rail service.
novelty_signature: Finite perched basalt aquifer allocated between continuous discharge to a wooded spring-run food web and mandatory dewatering of an aging regional rail tunnel; periphyton and detritus support insects, minnows, salamanders, kingfishers, and water snakes; ecological reservation closes the tunnel and imposes long ridge-road bus substitutions for three suburbs.
title: Aquifer reserve or drainage of a regional rail tunnel

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency

dilemma:
A state or provincial natural-resources agency must decide whether to renew the expiring lease of a worker cooperative operating the central ponds of a provincially owned saltworks estate. The estate lies between two remnant tidal marshes, and its levees, pumps, and truck causeways occupy the only low-elevation route connecting them to each other and to the estuary. If the agency declines renewal, it can breach levees, remove pumps and obstructing causeway sections, regrade the pond floors, excavate tidal creeks, and establish salt-marsh vegetation. Tides would then reconnect tidal creek, mudflat, salt marsh, and shallow lagoon habitats, carrying sediment, detritus, fish, invertebrates, and plant propagules through the former pond system.

Renewal would preserve the hydraulically isolated ponds required for commercial salt production. The cooperative would retain its contract-grade output, year-round workforce, buyer relationships, trucking activity, and the local spending that supports freight, repair, retail, and municipal revenue in a small town where it is the principal private employer. Restoration would end that production because the complete linked pond sequence is necessary to concentrate brine. Although transition funding, unemployment support, road access, and regional employment opportunities would prevent destitution or displacement, the town would face prolonged losses of specialized jobs, income, and interconnected business activity.

Should the agency choose habitat restoration that protects wetland continuity, or renew the lease to protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: A continuous elevation and salinity gradient of tidal creek, mudflat, salt marsh, and shallow lagoon habitat reconnects the two marsh remnants and the estuary. Daily tides again carry water, sediment, detritus, fish, invertebrates, and plant propagules through the converted central basin.
ecologically_protective_option: Decline lease renewal at the scheduled expiration, breach the seaward and cross-pond levees, remove pumps and obstructing causeway sections, regrade concentration and crystallizer floors, excavate branching tidal creeks, and establish locally sourced salt-marsh vegetation across the former pond train.
human_outcome_if_protected: The cooperative closes because restoration eliminates its productive pond sequence. A funded lease-end transition package, unemployment support, and regional road access prevent destitution or displacement, and some workers obtain other employment. Nevertheless, the town experiences prolonged losses of specialized jobs, household income, freight and repair demand, buyer relationships, retail spending, and predictable municipal revenue.
human_protective_option: Renew the cooperative's lease and maintain the hydraulically isolated sequence of leveed concentration ponds, crystallizers, pumps, and truck causeways required for commercial salt production.
novelty_signature: Provincially owned subtropical saltworks estate with abandoned outer ponds and an active worker-operated central pond train; levee breaching, regrading, and tidal-creek excavation restore continuous marsh, mudflat, and lagoon processes between two remnant wetlands; the same hydraulic isolation sustains sequential brine concentration; restoration closes a cooperative anchoring a small town's employment and service economy.
title: Restoring tidal continuity through a working salt landscape

dilemma:
A city-owned rocky foreshore contains the municipality’s only safely accessible tidepooling shore. For decades, families, school-age nature clubs, older naturalists, and residents without reliable private transport have used its intertidal pools for close observation, photography, species identification, and hands-on natural-history learning. The municipal council can either retain managed low-tide entry with visitor limits, designated access periods, and bans on collecting or handling organisms, or designate the entire platform a marine protected area and prohibit entry onto the rock for twelve years. Coastal walking and cliff-top viewing would remain available under closure, but users would lose access to the pools themselves, and distant shores are not a practical replacement for regular local outings.

Visitors must cross the central mussel and algal bands along a few gently sloped safe routes. Repeated foot placement crushes mussel and snail recruits and dislodges canopy algae, leaving bare corridors that become hotter and drier at low tide. These corridors fragment mussel beds, shaded crevices, and pool-edge cover, preventing recovery of grazers, filter feeders, predators, crustaceans, and juvenile fish that use the reef as an interacting community. Five years of capped access, walking lines, and monitoring did not stop the damage. A twelve-year closure would allow mussels and canopy algae to regain continuous cover and reconnect the moisture-retaining habitat on which the community depends.

Should the municipal council choose the protected-area closure that restores the marine ecosystem or managed access that preserves regular hands-on tidepool recreation?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Juvenile mussels and canopy algae survive across the former walking corridors until they form continuous cover. Moisture-retaining crevices and shaded pool margins reconnect, allowing grazers, filter feeders, predators, crustaceans, and refuge-using juvenile fish to recover as an interacting intertidal community.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the entire reef platform as a marine protected area and prohibit entry onto the intertidal rock for twelve years, while retaining access to the landward cliff path and viewing points. Twelve years is the surveyed period needed for mussel cohorts and canopy algae to re-establish continuous cover across the damaged corridors under local recruitment rates.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents can continue coastal walking and view the platform from the cliff path, but they lose twelve years of moving among pools, observing submerged organisms at close range, practicing shore identification, photographing pool life, and teaching children practical natural history at the city’s only safely accessible tidepooling site.
human_protective_option: Retain managed low-tide entry, with daily visitor limits, designated access periods, and bans on collecting or intentionally handling organisms, so regular hands-on tidepool recreation can continue.
novelty_signature: City-owned rocky intertidal platform; family and naturalist tidepooling; unavoidable foot placement along limited safe lines fragments mussel beds and algal canopies into heat-exposed corridors; twelve-year whole-platform marine protected-area closure restores a connected multi-species shore community while ending the municipality’s only regularly accessible hands-on tidepool recreation.
title: Closure of a trampling-sensitive intertidal reef platform

dilemma:
A nationally owned barrier island contains a degraded dune neck separating the only two surviving patches of an island-endemic burrowing skink. The neck is the only terrain that can be restored into connected loose-sand habitat. Tamarisk windbreaks, a stone platform and stabilizing apron, and compacted ceremonial approaches now hold the sand in place. Removing them, recontouring the area, and restoring sparse native dune cover would allow wind to move sand through the neck again, reconnecting feeding, breeding, shelter, and dispersal habitat across most of the skink’s remaining potential range.

The stone platform is also the inherited setting for a midsummer signal-fire ceremony shared by five coastal communities. Families carry embers from their household hearths, light a large beacon, exchange songs with answering fires visible across the strait, and return the fire to their community halls. The rite renews shared ancestry and reciprocal obligations. Restoring the dune would prohibit the gathering and large fire, ending the unified, place-based ceremony; songs and separate local fires could continue, but not the reciprocal beacon sequence. Retaining the platform, windbreaks, hardened access, and fire-control clearing would preserve the ceremony but leave the skink patches small and isolated, with little movement through the neck.

Should the national government choose dune restoration to protect the endemic skink or retain the site to protect the communities’ cultural practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Wind again moves sand through the neck, producing a connected mosaic of loose burrowing substrate and shifting native cover. This reconnects the two surviving skink patches and restores feeding, breeding, shelter, and dispersal habitat across most of the species' remaining potential range.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the tamarisk windbreaks, dismantle the platform's stabilizing apron, loosen and recontour compacted approaches, restore wind-scoured sand movement, establish sparse locally native dune vegetation, and prohibit the beacon gathering and large fire within the restored neck.
human_outcome_if_protected: The five communities lose the inherited gathering at the platform and the simultaneous sequence of carrying household embers, lighting the shared beacon, receiving visible acknowledgment from every shore, and returning the fire to community halls. Songs and separate local fires could continue, but the unified cross-strait rite and its place-based renewal of intercommunity obligations would end.
human_protective_option: Retain the windbreak, stone platform, stabilizing apron, fire-control clearing, and hardened access route; renew the annual gathering and fire permit; and forgo restoration of a continuous dynamic-sand corridor through the neck.
novelty_signature: National barrier-island dune neck; island-endemic burrowing skink isolated between two loose-sand patches; removal of tamarisk, stone apron, and compacted approaches to restore wind-driven sand connectivity; conflict with a five-community midsummer signal-fire involving household embers, simultaneous cross-strait visibility, answering songs, and reciprocal obligations.
title: Dune restoration at an ancestral signal-fire ground

dilemma:
In a temperate lake basin, twelve family orchard owners operate mature apple and pear parcels on the lower terraces of six tributaries. Their post-bloom insecticide applications are carried by scheduled irrigation into subsurface tile drains, producing repeated pulses in the tributaries that are lethal to sensitive mayfly, stonefly, and caddisfly larvae. These insects are a seasonal food source for juvenile native fish, and their emergence supports feeding by bats and nesting swallows. If the pulses continue, the tributary network remains dominated by tolerant organisms, with weakened links among aquatic insects, fish, and aerial insectivores.

The river-basin authority can prohibit the insecticide in the mapped source area for nine years, allowing aquatic-insect and fish cohorts to recover. But without it, internal pest damage exceeds fresh-market buyer tolerances. Transition grants would prevent foreclosure and support debt restructuring and gradual replanting, yet the owners would lose years of ordinary orchard income, much of the productive value of mature trees, and part of their equity in the jointly owned grading and cold-storage facility.

Alternatively, the authority can renew licensed applications at existing rates and setbacks. The orchards would retain saleable yields, and the mature trees, parcels, and specialized facility would preserve their established agricultural and collateral value, while the tributary food web would remain impaired. Should the river-basin authority choose the prohibition that protects trophic integrity or renew the pesticide use that protects the orchard owners’ property?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Sensitive mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies recover across the tributary network. Their restored larval and emergence biomass supports juvenile native fish, improves recruitment into larger fish age classes, and increases dependable stream-corridor feeding opportunities for insectivorous bats and nesting swallows.
ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit use of the insecticide throughout the mapped source area for nine years. This period covers establishment of replacement orchard blocks and allows multiple aquatic-insect and native-fish cohorts to recover under continued monitoring.
human_outcome_if_protected: Without the insecticide, internal pest damage in the established dessert-fruit cultivars remains above regional fresh-market buyer tolerances. Owners retain their homes and land, and transition grants prevent insolvency and fund debt restructuring and gradual replanting, but they lose several years of ordinary orchard income, much of the remaining productive value of mature trees, and part of their equity in a volume-dependent grading and cold-storage facility.
human_protective_option: Renew licensed post-bloom applications at existing rates and setbacks, preserving commercially saleable fruit yields and the productive value of the mature orchards, grading facility, and cold-storage property.
novelty_signature: Temperate apple-and-pear tributary belt; irrigation-driven tile-drain pulses of a post-bloom insecticide; aquatic-insect emergence linking juvenile fish, larger fish, bats, and swallows; mature dessert-fruit trees and jointly owned grading and cold-storage property; concealed internal-fruit pest, distributed drain outlets, and landscape recolonization defeating temporal, buffer, end-of-pipe, and partial-treatment compromises.
title: Mayfly-safe insecticide rule for an orchard tributary belt

dilemma:
A regional government must decide whether to cancel a planned extension of the airport runway serving a roadless subarctic settlement. The extension would add a freight apron, approach-light corridor, and wildlife-exclusion fence across the only broad, low-gradient passage between coastal caribou calving grounds and inland winter range. Steep broken ground and thaw-sensitive wetlands constrain movement around it. If the project is cancelled, the existing short, unfenced gravel runway will remain in use, leaving the passage open for caribou to migrate, disperse, mix between regional groups, and recolonize areas after difficult winters.

If the government authorizes construction, larger cargo aircraft will be able to carry substantially greater refrigerated and palletized freight throughout the year. Stores will restock weekly, recurring gaps in produce, eggs, dairy, and other ordinary foods will decline, and lower freight costs will reduce prices. Without the extension, households—especially low- and moderate-income families—will continue facing high food prices, limited variety, less frequent refrigerated deliveries, and multi-day gaps in fresh foods, though subsidies, reserve stocks, and emergency flights will preserve adequate nutrition.

Should the regional government cancel the runway extension to protect habitat connectivity for caribou, or construct it to improve reliable, affordable food access for settlement households?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Caribou can continue moving through the sole low-gradient passage between complementary seasonal ranges. Groups using adjacent parts of the regional range remain able to mix, disperse, and recolonize areas after difficult winters, supporting a connected rather than subdivided population.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the runway extension, freight apron, approach-light corridor, and new perimeter fence while continuing to operate the existing short, unfenced runway. This leaves the full width of the established passage available to moving caribou.
human_outcome_if_protected: Stores remain dependent on small turboprop deliveries with low payload limits and frequent weather-related cancellations. Freight charges remain substantially higher, refrigerated shipments arrive less often, and multi-day gaps in produce, eggs, and dairy continue. Staple subsidies, reserve stocks, and emergency small-aircraft deliveries preserve sufficient calories, so cancellation does not cause hunger, forced movement, or severe physical harm.
human_protective_option: Construct the longer runway, freight apron, approach-light corridor, and required wildlife-exclusion fence, enabling aircraft with substantially larger pallet and refrigerated-freight capacity to serve the settlement throughout the year.
novelty_signature: Roadless subarctic settlement; cancellation of a regional cargo-runway extension; required wildlife fencing and aviation disturbance span the sole low-gradient caribou passage between seasonal ranges; continued small-turboprop dependence preserves adequate calories but causes high grocery prices, limited refrigerated volume, and recurring fresh-food gaps.
title: Cancel a tundra cargo-runway extension across a caribou passage

dilemma:
An environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to renew the operating permissions for an old navigation dam retrofitted with hydropower turbines in a postindustrial river district. The dam divides three surviving beds of native river mussels. Their larvae disperse only while attached to migratory redhorse fish, but the dam and its eight-kilometre deep, slow, fine-sediment reservoir prevent the fish from moving effectively among the reaches and eliminate the flowing-shoal habitat needed for mussel recruitment. Each bed contains uncommon alleles associated with shell strength, temperature tolerance, and parasite resistance. If the dam remains, the beds will stay isolated, and drift and inbreeding will progressively reduce regional genetic diversity.

The agency may deny renewal and require removal of the dam, navigation sill, turbines, and sediment plug, restoring a free-flowing channel. Redhorse would then again carry larvae among all three beds, maintaining gene exchange and those uncommon traits in a connected mussel population. Yet removal would permanently end the public utility’s low-cost power allocation. Under its established replacement contract, household bills would rise materially and persistently; food processors would stagger operations away from costly evening periods, while public charging sites and repair workshops would reduce evening hours. Essential electricity, safe heating, and food-safety refrigeration would remain available.

Should the environmental regulatory agency require dam removal to protect genetic diversity or renew the permissions to protect affordable, predictable energy access?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Migratory redhorse can again move through all three reaches carrying mussel larvae. Successful recruitment among the beds restores gene exchange and maintains uncommon functional alleles as part of a connected regional mussel population.
ecologically_protective_option: Refuse renewal of the facility's operating permissions and require removal of the dam, navigation sill, turbines, and accumulated fine-sediment plug, followed by stabilization of released sediment and restoration of a free-flowing channel.
human_outcome_if_protected: The utility replaces the lost allocation through its documented least-cost regional power contract. Household bills rise materially and persistently. Food processors stagger refrigeration, washing, and cleaning cycles away from expensive evening periods, while public charging sites and repair workshops reduce evening hours. Essential household electricity, safe heating, and continuous food-safety refrigeration remain available.
human_protective_option: Renew the operating permissions and retain the dam and generation, preserving the public utility's low-cost power allocation and current evening supply schedule.
novelty_signature: Retrofitted industrial navigation dam; host-fish-mediated gene exchange among three native mussel beds; redhorse passage failure combined with an eight-kilometre fine-sediment reservoir break; postindustrial public utility losing allocated low-cost power; recurring tariff increases and staggered refrigeration, charging, and workshop schedules.
title: Removing an industrial-river hydropower dam to reconnect native mussel breeding beds

dilemma:
A public land-management authority must decide whether to impose a twelve-year ban on taking clams and other burrowing shellfish from a centuries-continuous eelgrass meadow in an estuarine reserve. The meadow’s interwoven rhizome mat, shell deposits, tidal microchannels, sediment gradients, and patch-specific benthic communities are mature structures that cannot be recreated quickly. Continued hand-digging, even under current bag limits, approved tools, and hole-filling rules, creates pits and cuts rhizomes. Winter waves enlarge nearby pits into erosional gaps, fragmenting the connected meadow mosaic. With twelve undisturbed years, scars can regain the mature meadow’s rhizome density, elevation, and benthic assemblages.

The ban would stop new digging damage while retaining boardwalk viewing, shoreline access, and non-harvest observation. Yet it would prohibit entry onto the vegetated flat for digging, removing the only nearby, firm, safely walkable public clam-harvesting ground for residents of three coastal towns. Older adults and families regularly use the site to dig clams, teach harvesting skills, and prepare shared weekend meals. Other flats are dangerously soft or require private boats, so they are not practical alternatives for many users. Renewing permits would preserve this frequent, affordable, intergenerational recreation but allow the meadow’s fragmentation to continue.

Should the public land-management authority choose the twelve-year harvest ban to protect the old-growth ecosystem, or renew permits to protect residents’ recreational clam-digging?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: New digging scars and shellfish-removal disturbances cease. Existing pits gradually infill, rhizome edges recolonize damaged patches, sediment oxygen gradients restabilize, and the remaining rhizome, shell-layer, channel, and benthic-community mosaic avoids further fragmentation. Local recovery plots show that approximately twelve undisturbed years are needed for scarred areas to regain the mature meadow’s range of rhizome density, elevation, and benthic assemblages.
ecologically_protective_option: Impose a twelve-year ban on taking clams and other burrowing shellfish throughout the old-growth eelgrass meadow. Boardwalk viewing, shoreline access, and non-harvest observation remain allowed, but entry onto the vegetated intertidal flat for digging is prohibited.
human_outcome_if_protected: Residents lose the only nearby and safely walkable place where they can regularly engage in clam-digging, practical instruction, and catch preparation. They retain ordinary shore visits, boardwalk viewing, and other beach recreation, but boat-only grounds and dangerously soft flats do not provide a usable substitute for many older adults and families.
human_protective_option: Renew recreational hand-harvest permits under the existing daily bag limits, approved short-tined tools, and hole-filling requirements, allowing residents to continue clam-digging on the meadow’s firm margin.
novelty_signature: Public estuarine reserve containing a centuries-continuous eelgrass rhizome, shell-layer, channel, and benthic-community mosaic; twelve-year ban on recreational clam and burrowing-shellfish harvest; lawful hand-digging pits coalesce under winter waves into erosional gaps; three towns lose their only firm, safely walkable public site for intergenerational clam-digging recreation.
title: Clam-harvest ban in a long-continuous eelgrass meadow

dilemma:
Five towns share a river delta whose seasonally flooded clay meadows form the only continuous low-elevation transition between inland reed marshes and brackish coastal wetlands. As existing clay-extraction permits near expiry, an intermunicipal public authority must decide whether to designate this corridor a no-extraction zone or renew phased extraction permissions for twenty years.

Prohibiting further pits, dewatering ditches, spoil bunds, and haul roads would retain the continuous band of shallow-flooded meadow. Its moisture and salinity gradient would continue to sustain characteristic meadow plant zonation and the movement of insects, amphibians, floodplain fish during inundation, seeds, detritus, and fine sediment among the wetland zones. But when permits expire, local clay extraction would end. Two roof-tile kilns would lose the clay blend required by their equipment and certified products, and linked digging, haulage, finishing, and sales firms would lose recurring work. Grants and employment assistance would limit material hardship, yet specialized careers, family-firm income, productive assets, and business value would be lost.

Renewing extraction would preserve the established tile-production cluster, skilled jobs, contracts, and family businesses for twenty years. Successive pits and their required drainage and road structures, however, would replace the continuous seasonal meadow gradient with deep permanent ponds and dry barriers, disrupting wet-meadow habitat and lateral flow between the inland and coastal wetlands. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the no-extraction zone that protects wetland continuity or renew extraction to protect local livelihoods?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The remaining continuous band of seasonally shallow-flooded meadow is retained between the reed marshes and brackish wetlands. Its moisture and salinity gradient continues to support meadow plant zonation and the movement or transport of wetland insects, amphibians, floodplain fish during inundation, seeds, detritus, and fine sediment.
ecologically_protective_option: Designate the wet-meadow corridor as a no-extraction land-use zone, deny renewal of expiring clay permits, prohibit new pits, dewatering ditches, spoil bunds, and haul roads, and restore disturbed parcel edges where the original meadow substrate remains.
human_outcome_if_protected: When current permits expire, local extraction ends. The two kilns lose the clay blend for which their equipment and certified products are configured; linked finishing and haulage firms lose recurring work. Transition grants and general employment assistance limit material hardship, but workers lose specialized careers and family firms lose income, productive assets, and saleable business value.
human_protective_option: Renew phased extraction and associated haul-road permissions for twenty years, allowing the two tile kilns and linked digging, haulage, finishing, and sales businesses to continue at their established scale.
novelty_signature: Five-town river-delta wet-meadow transition between inland reed marsh and brackish coastal wetlands; intermunicipal no-extraction zoning; shallow clay pits, dewatering ditches, spoil bunds, and haul roads replace a seasonal shallow gradient with deep ponds and dry barriers; deposit-specific certified roof-tile livelihood cluster.
title: Clay-extraction prohibition in a delta wet-meadow corridor

dilemma:
Each summer, a municipal council must assign the fixed output of its tertiary-treatment plant. The available reclaimed water can either be sent through subsurface infiltration basins to a protected dune field or used to irrigate a long-established neighborhood garden. Supplying the monitored minimum volume to the dunes would maintain the shallow seasonal groundwater range that sustains their native sedges, rushes, orchids, mint, and annual wetland herbs. The slacks would retain their alternating wet and moist zones, allowing orchids and wetland annuals to flower and recruit rather than giving way to dry scrub and invasive grasses.

The same allocation would end summer deliveries to the garden used by several hundred families for a four-generation diaspora New Year practice. Reliable irrigation presently permits coordinated planting and watering, teaching in the fields, cultivation of selected herbs and vegetables, seed saving and exchange, and a collective harvest. Families could still obtain food, meet, cook shared recipes, and observe the New Year date, but purchased produce would not preserve the shared growing and harvest cycle or the locally maintained seed lines. The water supply cannot meet both minimum needs: a split would cause the dune community’s central recruitment zone and the garden’s long-season crops and seed crop to fail.

Should the municipal council allocate the water to protect the native dune-slack plant community or to protect the garden-based cultural practice?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The slacks retain alternating shallow-inundation and moist-drawdown zones. Native orchids and annual wetland herbs can flower and recruit, sedges and rushes retain their moisture zones, and the characteristic slack mosaic avoids conversion to dry scrub and invasive grasses.
ecologically_protective_option: Allocate the monitored minimum summer volume to the dune infiltration basins, maintaining the seasonal groundwater range required by the native slack community, and discontinue summer reclaimed-water deliveries to the garden.
human_outcome_if_protected: Families retain access to ordinary food, meeting space, cooking gatherings, and the New Year date, but cannot complete the local growing cycle around which field instruction, seed selection, exchange, and collective harvest are organized. Purchased plants and produce allow recipes to be prepared but do not continue the shared cultivation-and-harvest component or maintain the locally adapted seed lines.
