dilemma:
A silty temperate embayment supports connected eelgrass beds, shell beds, benthic invertebrates, juvenile fish, and their predators. Two passenger-and-vehicle ferries berth there and repeatedly cross shallow nursery waters while serving inhabited islands. Monitoring identifies their copper-antifouling hull coatings as the principal controllable source of chronic copper exposure around the terminals and sailing corridor. If a provincial natural-resources agency denies renewal of the coatings’ permit, new copper loading will fall below the locally established effects level. Amphipods, juvenile bivalves, and eelgrass-surface grazers will recover, strengthening filtration, grazing, decomposition, and fish-prey relationships throughout the embayment’s connected community.

The restriction would require both ferries to use a nonbiocidal barrier coating and undergo repeated mechanical cleaning at a mainland yard during the roughly four-month high-fouling season. Staggered withdrawals and weather-related yard delays would reduce service from hourly departures to roughly every three hours on recurring days for eight years. Island residents—including commuters, students, patients attending routine appointments, caregivers, and tradespeople—would still have ferry service, but would face reservations, constrained vehicle capacity, missed connections, and longer routine trips. Renewing the permit would preserve hourly departures and current capacity, but copper exposure would continue to suppress sensitive invertebrates and leave eelgrass-edge and shell-bed communities simplified across a substantial part of the embayment.

Should the provincial natural-resources agency deny the permit to protect the marine ecosystem or renew it to protect island residents’ mobility?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: New copper loading from the two hulls declines enough that monitored chronic exposure no longer exceeds the locally established effects level around the terminals and sailing corridor. Sensitive amphipods, juvenile bivalves, and eelgrass-surface grazers recover, strengthening grazing, filtration, decomposition, and fish-prey pathways across the connected eelgrass and shell-bed community.
ecologically_protective_option: Deny renewal of the copper-antifouling permit for both ferries. Require an abrasion-resistant, nonbiocidal epoxy barrier coating and scheduled mechanical removal of fouling at an equipped mainland yard.
human_outcome_if_protected: The nonbiocidal barrier coating prevents direct biocide release but does not stop organisms from attaching. During the roughly four-month high-fouling season, each vessel therefore requires repeated mainland-yard cleaning to remain within fuel-efficiency and inspection limits. Staggered withdrawals, compounded by weather-related yard delays, reduce departures from hourly to approximately every three hours on recurring days during that season for eight years. Residents retain service but face reservations, constrained vehicle capacity, missed mainland connections, and substantially longer routine trips.
human_protective_option: Renew the copper-antifouling permit, allowing both ferries to retain their current maintenance cycle and hourly service.
novelty_signature: Silty temperate island embayment; site-specific copper-antifouling pesticide permit for two continuously immersed passenger-and-vehicle ferries; chronic effects on eelgrass–shell-bed grazing, filtration, decomposition, and prey pathways; nonbiocidal barrier coating requires recurring mainland haul-outs that reduce island departures during the high-fouling season.
title: Copper-antifouling restriction for an island passenger ferry

dilemma:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to renew commercial licences for mature native rattan in a tropical upland’s mapped gorge-and-gap network. At a limited number of bottlenecks, long rattan canes are the only continuous routes between old-forest sections. If the council imposes a nine-year harvest ban, the existing living bridges will remain intact and younger canes will grow into additional crossings. Ground-averse arboreal mammals and lizards, as well as canopy-associated invertebrates that use the stems, will continue to disperse between breeding areas and recolonize forest patches after cyclone damage.

Renewing licences at the minimum volume needed by the shared workshop would require cutting the mature canes at those bottlenecks. The resulting openings exceed the focal animals’ crossing ability, reducing movement and post-storm recolonization and fragmenting previously connected populations into smaller habitat units. Yet a ban would also remove the workshop’s only local supply of furniture-grade cane. The workshop would close, skilled cutting and craft jobs would disappear, freight contracts would lapse, and retail trade would contract in both villages. Households would retain necessities through mixed livelihoods and transition payments, but not the trade’s skilled work, business value, or predictable cash income.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the nine-year harvest ban that protects habitat connectivity or renew the licences that protect local economic stability?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Existing living bridges remain at every mapped bottleneck, while younger canes develop additional overlap. Ground-averse arboreal mammals and lizards, together with canopy-associated invertebrates documented using the stems, can continue dispersing between breeding areas and recolonizing patches after cyclone damage.
ecologically_protective_option: Ban commercial harvesting of mature native rattan throughout the mapped gorge-and-gap network for nine years. Existing spanning canes must remain intact, and younger canes must be allowed to grow to crossing length before harvesting can be reconsidered.
human_outcome_if_protected: Without legal native-cane deliveries, the shared workshop closes, cutting and craft jobs disappear, freight contracts lapse, and retail activity contracts in both villages. Council transition payments, subsistence activities, and other mixed livelihoods preserve food, housing, and essential services, but do not replace skilled occupations, business equity, or predictable cash earnings during the nine-year period.
human_protective_option: Renew the existing licences at the documented minimum annual volume needed to keep the shared steaming and furniture workshop operating and retain its buyers, workforce, and freight contracts.
novelty_signature: Indigenous-governed monsoon upland; mature native rattan functioning as living canopy bridges across serial gorge and cyclone-gap bottlenecks; nine-year rattan harvest ban; arboreal dispersal and post-cyclone recolonization; two-village cutting, steaming, furniture, freight, and retail production chain.
title: Rattan bridges across a monsoon-forest gorge network

dilemma:
A national government must decide whether to remove a nationally owned hydropower dam in a mountain watershed. The dam’s reservoir inundates the principal waterfall gorge of the silver-thread caddisfly, which exists nowhere else. Only two small tributary spray patches still support the species. Removing the dam and permanently draining the reservoir would restore free flow, waterfalls, cold spray-wetted boulder faces, and continuous habitat through the gorge. This would reconnect the surviving populations and restore a substantial part of the caddisfly’s endemic range. Retaining the dam would leave the gorge submerged, keeping the species confined to isolated spray patches that shrink during dry years.

Twenty-six lawful owner and tenant households live on an ancient landslide bench beside the reservoir. Reservoir water stabilizes the submerged toe of the slide; permanent drawdown would cause progressive ground displacement that their homes, roads, water lines, and sewers cannot withstand. If the dam is removed, residents would receive secure replacement homes, moving expenses, and tenure protection in the same municipality before any movement occurs. Yet they would have to leave their current homes and compact neighborhood, losing direct proximity to the chapel and community hall and some established daily care and maintenance relationships. Retaining the dam would allow them to remain safely in their homes and preserve their neighborhood’s routines and support network.

Should the national government remove the dam to restore the endemic caddisfly’s habitat, or retain it so the households can remain in their current community?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: Restored waterfalls and spray-wetted rock support the caddisfly’s egg, larval, pupal, and adult habitat requirements across the principal gorge. Continuous suitable habitat reconnects the two surviving tributary populations and restores a substantial share of the species’ endemic range.
ecologically_protective_option: Remove the dam and associated powerworks, permanently drain the impoundment, and restore free flow through the gorge so its waterfalls, turbulent boulder faces, and cold spray zones re-form.
human_outcome_if_protected: Before drawdown, residents receive secure replacement homes, moving expenses, and tenure protection in the same municipality. A single nearby parcel cannot safely accommodate all households in their existing compact arrangement, so residents must leave the bench and lose their current homes, direct proximity to the chapel and community hall, and some daily neighbor-to-neighbor care and maintenance arrangements.
human_protective_option: Retain the dam and its established operating range, including the reservoir level needed to stabilize the landslide toe, so the households can remain safely in their current homes and neighborhood.
novelty_signature: National mountain-reservoir removal; watershed-endemic waterfall caddisfly surviving in two tributary spray patches; restoration of submerged falls and oxygenated spray-boulder habitat; reservoir buttressing of an inhabited ancient landslide bench; advance compensated relocation caused by progressive permanent drawdown displacement.
title: Drawdown of a mountain gorge reservoir above a slide-bench village

dilemma:
A storm destroyed the pedestrian pier linking a mainland public park to an offshore surf headland. The regional planning commission must decide whether to approve a continuous rock causeway with an elevated pedestrian deck or deny the authorizations required for construction. The causeway’s landing and storm-resistant abutment would occupy the headland’s only intact low dune neck, where foredune, wet-swale, and salt-spray populations of a native beach grass contain distinct genetic traits. Construction would remove most of the wet-swale breeding population and its seed bank, block storm overwash, and progressively dry and narrow the swale. Alleles concentrated in the wet-swale lineage, including waterlogging-response variants, would be lost, substantially reducing the species’ genetic breadth at the site.

Cancelling the project would leave the dune neck’s wind-driven sand movement and overwash intact, retaining the three populations and their differing burial, waterlogging, and salt tolerances. But the former pier cannot be repaired, and most members of two established surf clubs cannot safely cross the deep, current-swept channel while carrying boards. Without the causeway, youth instruction, older participants’ sessions, winter surfing, and spontaneous low-cost use of the sheltered break would largely end. Calm-weather boat trips and other beaches would remain available, but would not provide regular access for these activities.

Should the regional planning commission cancel the causeway to protect the beach grass’s genetic diversity, or approve it to restore dependable recreation for the surf clubs?
ecological_outcome_if_protected: The foredune, seasonally wet swale, and salt-spray ridge populations remain in place. Their documented differences in burial tolerance, waterlogging response, and salt tolerance are retained, while occasional pollen and seed movement continues among the three populations.
ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the planned causeway and elevated walkway, remove only the unsafe remains of the old pier from outside the dune neck, and leave the neck’s overwash and wind-driven sand movement intact.
human_outcome_if_protected: Most members lose regular access to the headland break. Calm-weather boat visits remain possible for a limited number of experienced surfers, and other regional beaches remain open, but neither option supports the clubs’ frequent youth instruction, older participants, winter sessions, or spontaneous low-cost use of their established local site.
human_protective_option: Approve and construct the causeway and elevated walkway, restoring dependable, low-cost pedestrian access for people carrying surfboards to the headland’s sheltered break.
novelty_signature: Storm-damaged pedestrian access to an offshore surf headland; genetically differentiated beach-grass populations across foredune, wet-swale, and salt-spray microhabitats; cancellation of a rock causeway whose landing removes a lineage and blocks overwash; community surf clubs lose dependable board-carrying access to a uniquely sheltered break.
title: Cancel an all-weather access causeway to a remote surf headland
